title: The chain: code, record, decision support, clinician, patient
description: A wrong code doesn't harm a patient by itself — it harms them by traveling, unchallenged, through a chain of systems and people who each trusted the step before them.

learningObjectives.text: Name the five links a code passes through before it can affect a patient
Identify which link in a given scenario was the point a harmful code could have been stopped

contentSections.title: One code, five links, one patient

contentSections.body: A penicillin allergy, documented in 2019 at an urgent care visit, gets coded during a chart abstraction as an intolerance to a completely different drug class. Nobody re-examines the original note. Three years and two hospital systems later, a resident orders amoxicillin for a straightforward sinus infection. The decision-support alert that should have fired stays silent, because the system is checking against the wrong allergen. Nothing about this required anyone to be careless. Every single person along the way did a reasonable thing with the information they were given.

contentSections.scenario: The chain that carried that error is: **the code itself** (what got entered) → **the record** (where it lives and how it's structured) → **decision support** (the rules that read the record) → **the clinician** (who acts on what decision support tells them, or doesn't) → **the patient** (who receives the order). Ask where the *initial* defect was introduced in the scenario above.
contentSections.question: Where did the actual error enter the chain?

options.label: At decision support — the alert should have caught it regardless of the code
At the coding step — the wrong allergen code was assigned during abstraction
At the clinician — they should have asked the patient directly about allergies

feedback.ds: Decision support is a downstream link, not the origin — it did exactly what it was built to do: check the code that was in the record. It has no way to know the code itself was wrong. Blaming the alert for not catching a bad input is a category error you'll see constantly in this work.
feedback.coding: Right. The chain didn't fail at the alert, or at the clinician — it failed at the moment a human or a tool assigned the wrong code to the original allergy note, years before anyone downstream touched it. Everything after that point was a system correctly propagating a wrong fact.
feedback.clinician: Asking the patient is good practice and would have caught this — but that's a *recovery* point, not where the error originated. The question is about the defect's origin, because that's where a fix actually has to land. A system that only relies on the last clinician catching every upstream error isn't a safety system, it's luck.

contentSections.concept: **Every harmful event has an origin point and one or more recovery points.** The origin is where the wrong fact was created. Recovery points are every later place someone or something *could have* caught it, and didn't. An audit that only looks at the recovery point closest to the patient — usually the clinician — will keep finding the same conclusion: "the doctor should have checked." That's true and also nearly useless, because it doesn't say anything about the four links before it.

contentSections.body:
Walk the five links in order, because the direction matters:

1. **The code** — what got assigned, by a human coder, an NLP-assisted tool, or both, and how confident that assignment actually was.
2. **The record** — where the code lives: a problem list, an allergy field, a medication list, a diagnosis on a claim. The same wrong code does very different damage depending which of these it lands in.
3. **Decision support** — the rule engines that read structured data and fire (or stay silent): allergy checking, drug interaction checking, dosing checks, sepsis alerts.
4. **The clinician** — who is shown an alert, or isn't, and who has seconds to decide whether to trust it, override it, or investigate further.
5. **The patient** — who receives whatever the previous four links produced.

A reviewer's job in this module is not to find the mistake. It's to find *which link* the mistake entered at, and every link after it that had a chance to stop it and didn't.

contentSections.question: If a health system fixed only the clinician-facing alert screen — making every allergy alert louder and harder to dismiss — but never touched how allergy codes get assigned during chart abstraction, what would actually happen to the amoxicillin scenario from the hook?
contentSections.answer: Nothing would change. The alert never fired in the first place because the underlying code was wrong — there was no alert to make louder. A louder-alert fix targets a link the error never reached; the defect sits one link further upstream, at coding.
contentSections.hint: Ask which link in the chain the fix is aimed at, and which link the actual defect lives in.

contentSections.body: A harmful code has an origin link and a series of recovery links. Fixing the person closest to the patient without fixing the origin just moves the failure point downstream to the next chart.

contentSections.title: Reading a chain backwards from the harm

contentSections.body: A safety report lands on your desk that says only: "Patient received wrong-strength medication; contributing factor, EHR coding error." That sentence names an outcome and gestures at a cause. It does not name a chain. Your job is to rebuild the chain the sentence is hiding.

contentSections.scenario: A 68-year-old with chronic kidney disease is admitted. Her problem list carries "CKD stage 2" — a code left over from a lab result four years old, never updated despite two more recent labs showing stage 4. A renally-dosed antibiotic order goes through decision support, which checks the coded stage and finds no dosing conflict for stage 2. The full adult dose is given. The patient develops acute kidney injury.
contentSections.question: What is the root mechanism that let this reach the patient?

options.label: The antibiotic itself was inappropriate for a CKD patient
A stale, uncorrected code on the problem list fed a decision-support check that was otherwise working correctly
The clinician failed to check kidney function before ordering

feedback.drug: The drug is appropriate for CKD patients — at a reduced dose. The problem isn't the choice of drug, it's that the system checking the dose was working off a stage of kidney disease that was four years stale. Fix the drug choice and the same code still poisons the next order.
feedback.stale: Yes. The decision-support rule itself worked exactly as designed — it checked the coded stage against the dosing table and found no conflict. The mechanism that failed was upstream: nothing in the record-keeping process re-derives or timestamps a problem-list code against new lab evidence, so a four-year-old "stage 2" sat there looking current.
feedback.clinician: Checking kidney function directly would have caught this, and it's a fair habit to want — but treating this as a clinician failure alone misses that the whole point of coded decision support is to make that manual check unnecessary in the common case. If the system is going to carry the coded fact, the coded fact has to be trustworthy, or the system is worse than no system.

contentSections.mechanism: **A stale or unreviewed code is functionally a wrong code**, even if it was correct the day it was entered. Decision support has no concept of "this used to be true." It reads what's coded right now and trusts it completely. The mechanism to look for in an audit isn't always "who typed the wrong thing" — very often it's "what should have re-evaluated this and didn't."

contentSections.body: This is why tracing the chain matters more than finding the culprit. "A coding error contributed to harm" describes almost every incident in this phase and explains almost none of them. The trace has to answer: which link introduced the defect, which links propagated it unchanged, and which link had a real chance to catch it and, for a specific, nameable reason, didn't. That third question is where your findings will eventually point — not at a person, at a gap in the chain.

contentSections.question: A safety report says "EHR coding error contributed to harm" and nothing else. Before you've traced anything, what's the single most useful next question to ask the person who wrote it?
contentSections.answer: "Which specific field or code, and where in the chain did it first appear?" — not "whose fault was it," and not "what happened to the patient." Everything else in the trace depends on locating the origin first; asking about outcome or blame before origin just produces a longer version of the same unhelpful headline.
contentSections.hint: The report already tells you the outcome. What it doesn't tell you is where the chain actually started.

contentSections.body: "EHR coding error contributed to harm" is a headline, not an analysis. The trace is: where did it start, what carried it unchanged, and where was the real chance to stop it.

title: Problem lists that follow a patient for years
description: A problem list is meant to be curated, but in practice it accretes — and a code that was reasonable once can sit uncorrected for years, quietly steering every system that reads it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why problem lists tend to accumulate stale or duplicate codes rather than staying curated
Identify the downstream systems that silently trust an uncurated problem list

contentSections.body: Open almost any patient with more than five years in the same health system and you'll find a problem list longer than their actual current problems: a resolved pneumonia from 2018 still active, "rule out" diagnoses that were never ruled anything, the same hypertension entered twice under two slightly different codes because two different visits generated two different notes.

contentSections.scenario: In audits of long-tenure patients' problem lists in large health systems, researchers have repeatedly found a meaningful share of "active" problems to be resolved, duplicated, or otherwise no longer accurate.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of entries on a typical long-tenure patient's problem list turn out, on audit, to be stale, duplicate, or no longer active?
contentSections.explanation: Published chart-audit studies commonly find somewhere in the range of a quarter to a third of "active" problem list entries are actually resolved, duplicated, or otherwise inaccurate — the exact number varies by system and specialty, but it is never close to zero, and it never trends downward on its own. A problem list is a write-mostly structure: adding is easy and rewarded (it documents acuity, supports billing, covers liability), removing requires someone to notice, decide, and act, with no similar reward for doing it.

contentSections.body:
Three forces push problem lists toward accumulation rather than accuracy, and none of them are anyone being lazy:

- **Adding is a single click; resolving is a judgment call.** A clinician entering a new diagnosis during a visit is doing exactly what the visit requires. Going back to close out an old, unrelated problem from a different specialty is a task nobody's workflow asks for.
- **Every specialist adds through their own lens.** A cardiologist, an endocrinologist and a primary care physician looking at the same chronic kidney disease may each code it slightly differently — different specificity, sometimes different code entirely — and none of them owns cleaning up the others' entries.
- **Coded problems support billing, and billing rewards presence, not accuracy.** A code that documents higher acuity can support a higher-complexity visit or a risk-adjustment payment. There's a real incentive to add and essentially none to prune, which is worth naming plainly rather than pretending it isn't there.
A problem list accumulates by default. Nothing in the ordinary workflow removes an entry — only adds one — so "it's on the list" is never, by itself, evidence that it's current.
The problem list looks like documentation. Structurally, it behaves like an input.

contentSections.scenario: Consider a stale "active" diagnosis of major depressive disorder, resolved years ago but never marked resolved, sitting on a patient's problem list.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually reads and acts on that coded entry, as opposed to just displaying it?

items.label: Risk-adjustment / HCC scoring used for payment models
Depression-screening decision support that may suppress a routine screen because a diagnosis is already "active"
Medication reconciliation logic that can flag or fail to flag a psychiatric medication as appropriate to the coded condition
The after-visit summary printer, which just prints whatever's on the list
Referral-triage tools that weight urgency partly on coded comorbidity burden

explanation.risk_adjust: Yes — risk-adjustment models read active diagnosis codes directly and a stale one can misstate a patient's coded acuity for a full payment year, independent of anything clinical happening to the patient.
explanation.cds_screen: Yes, and this is the sharpest patient-safety angle: some screening logic treats "already diagnosed" as a reason to skip a repeat screen. A resolved depression code sitting active can mean a genuinely at-risk patient never gets re-screened, because the system believes the question is already answered.
explanation.med_recon: Yes — reconciliation tools that try to match medications to indications use the problem list as their source of truth for what a medication is "for." A stale diagnosis can make an unrelated new prescription look justified, or a legitimately new concern look redundant.
explanation.printer: No — the after-visit summary is a display surface. It shows the patient what's on the list, but it doesn't feed any downstream decision. Harmless in the sense this module cares about, though confusing to the patient in its own way.
explanation.referral_ai: Yes — triage and prioritization tools that weight coded comorbidity burden will treat a stale severe diagnosis as current risk, which can misdirect scarce specialist capacity toward a problem that no longer exists.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern worth remembering: anything that only *displays* the problem list is low-stakes. Anything that *scores, screens, reconciles, or prioritizes* off it inherits every stale entry as if it were true today. An audit has to ask, for each stale entry you find, not "is this embarrassing" but "what reads this, and what does it do with what it reads."

contentSections.question: A patient portal shows a resolved diagnosis as still "active." The patient is confused and calls the clinic. From this module's framework, is that phone call itself a patient-safety event?
contentSections.answer: Not on its own — the portal is a display surface, and confusion without a downstream action isn't the kind of harm this phase tracks. But treat the call as a free signal: it's evidence the same stale code exists in the structured problem list, which almost certainly IS read by something that scores or screens off it. Follow the signal upstream rather than just correcting the portal display.
contentSections.hint: Separate the discomfort the patient feels from whether any system actually acted differently because of the stale code.

contentSections.body: A stale problem-list entry is inert on a printed summary and active everywhere a system scores, screens, or reconciles off it. Trace what actually reads the code before deciding how much the staleness matters.

title: Allergy and medication data: the fastest path to harm
description: Of every field a coder or an AI tool touches, allergy and medication data has the shortest, most direct line to a bad outcome — often minutes, not years.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why allergy and medication data carries higher immediate risk than most other coded fields
Distinguish a true allergy-coding error from a legitimate ambiguity a coder correctly flagged

contentSections.body: A wrong diagnosis code on a problem list can sit for years before it changes anything a clinician does. A wrong allergy code can change an order within the same encounter it was entered — sometimes within the same hour.

contentSections.scenario: A patient's discharge note from an outside hospital says "reports nausea with codeine, tolerates other opioids fine." The AI-assisted coding tool abstracting this note into the new system's structured allergy field enters it as: **Allergy: Opiates (class) — severity: unspecified**.
contentSections.question: What's the actual defect here?

options.label: Nothing — codeine is an opiate, so this is accurate
A drug-specific intolerance (nausea, not a true allergy) got generalized to an entire drug class
The severity should have been marked "severe" to be safe

feedback.fine: Codeine is an opiate, but the note explicitly says the patient tolerates *other* opioids — that sentence is the whole clinical content, and it's exactly what got dropped. The structured entry now says the opposite of what the source note says.
feedback.generalized: Right, and it's a two-part error. First, class-level generalization from a single-drug reaction is a documented, common failure mode — codeine intolerance does not imply hydromorphone intolerance, and the note said so directly. Second, nausea is a side effect, not an allergy; folding it into a structured "Allergy" field with no distinction from a true hypersensitivity reaction removes information a clinician needs to weigh risk. The result: an entire class of pain control is now flagged unavailable for a patient who tolerates most of it fine.
feedback.severity: Marking it more severe doesn't fix the underlying error — it makes a wrong, overgeneralized entry *more* confidently wrong. The fix isn't a more cautious severity, it's not generalizing past what the source note actually said.

contentSections.concept: **Allergy and medication fields have almost no tolerance for generalization**, because decision support treats them as hard stops, not soft signals. A diagnosis code that's slightly too broad might change how a chart looks. An allergy code that's too broad removes real treatment options — sometimes options that matter most in an emergency, when nobody has time to go find the original note and re-read it.

contentSections.body:
The distinction that matters for review is **intolerance versus allergy versus no reaction at all**, and it needs to survive the trip from free text into a structured field:

- **True allergy** — an immune-mediated reaction: hives, anaphylaxis, swelling. Genuinely a hard stop for that drug and often its close relatives.
- **Intolerance** — a side effect the patient dislikes or can't handle: nausea, sedation, a rash from a topical irritant. Clinically important, but not the same category, and should not silently trigger the same alerts a true allergy would.
- **No reaction, wrongly inferred from proximity** — a drug mentioned in the same paragraph as a reaction, coded as if it caused it. This one is purely a text-extraction failure, and it's exactly the kind of thing NLP-assisted abstraction tools produce when a note is dense and the reviewer skims past the field.

Allergy and medication fields don't have room for "close enough." Generalizing a single-drug intolerance into a class-level allergy removes real treatment options from a chart that may need them urgently.

A medication list error rarely announces itself. It shows up as a drug interaction check that should have fired and didn't, or one that fires so often on garbage entries that a clinician learns to click through it without reading.

contentSections.code:
Medication list entry, auto-populated from an outside pharmacy feed:

  Drug: "METOPROLOL TAR 25MG TAB"
  Coded as: Metolazone 25mg

(RxNorm mapping selected the nearest string match; no clinician review flagged before reconciliation was marked complete.)
contentSections.question: What's the core failure here?

options.label: The abbreviation "TAR" (tartrate) confused a string-matching mapper into picking a different, similarly-spelled drug entirely
25mg is an unusual dose for metoprolol
The outside pharmacy feed shouldn't be trusted at all

feedback.dose: 25mg is an entirely ordinary metoprolol tartrate dose — nothing about the quantity should have raised suspicion on its own, which is part of why this slipped through: nothing about the number looked wrong.
feedback.string: Yes. Metoprolol and metolazone are a beta-blocker and a diuretic — different drug classes, different purposes, different interaction profiles — but they're close enough as strings that a mapper leaning on text similarity rather than a verified code table can select the wrong RxNorm concept. This is a known, recurring failure pattern in medication reconciliation: look-alike drug names defeating automated matching, the same problem that's plagued paper prescribing for decades, now automated.
feedback.feed: The feed itself did its job — it passed along what the pharmacy had on file. The failure is entirely in how that text got mapped to a structured code, and in the fact that reconciliation was marked complete without a human catching a mapping that changed the actual drug.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Look-alike, sound-alike drug name confusion is one of the oldest documented categories of medication error, and mapping free text to a coded drug concept doesn't remove that risk — it just relocates it from a pharmacist's eye to a string-matching algorithm's confidence score. A reconciliation process that marks itself "complete" without a step that specifically checks *class* and *purpose* against what the patient is actually being treated for will pass this kind of error straight through. The tell, when you're auditing, is a mapped drug whose therapeutic class doesn't match anything else in the patient's problem list or med history — that mismatch is cheap to check for and catches a disproportionate share of these.

contentSections.question: The metoprolol/metolazone mix-up would have been caught immediately by a check comparing the mapped drug's class against what else is on the patient's chart. Why isn't that check universal in reconciliation tools already, if it's this cheap?
contentSections.answer: It usually requires the problem list to be reasonably accurate to compare against — and per this module's earlier lesson, problem lists are frequently stale or incomplete themselves. A class-consistency check is genuinely cheap to run, but it's only as good as the record it's checking against, which is exactly why coding quality upstream and downstream keep turning out to be the same problem.
contentSections.hint: The check itself is simple. What does it depend on that this module has already shown you can't be assumed reliable?

contentSections.body: Medication-list mapping errors most often come from look-alike names defeating a string match, not from anything wrong with the dose or the source feed. Check whether the mapped drug's class fits the rest of the chart.

title: Alerts that fire on bad data, and the fatigue that follows
description: A wrong code doesn't just cause silence where an alert should fire — it also causes noise, and the noise is what teaches clinicians to stop reading alerts at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the mechanism connecting coding errors to alert fatigue
Evaluate whether a specific alert-firing pattern reflects a genuine risk or a data-quality problem

contentSections.body: Everyone thinks about the alert that should have fired and didn't. Fewer people think about the alert that fires constantly on bad data, because that one doesn't look like a safety event — it looks like normal, if annoying, clinical software.

contentSections.question: A duplicate allergy entry — the same drug coded twice under two slightly different RxNorm concepts from two different visits — sits on a patient's chart. What's the most likely practical effect on decision support, versus what most people guess?
contentSections.answer: It usually causes the interaction/allergy check to fire twice for the same order, or fire on a near-miss that isn't real — training the clinician to expect noise from that patient's chart specifically, which is worse than firing once correctly.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a rules engine does when it finds two matching-but-not-identical entries, not one clean one.

contentSections.body:
The mechanism runs like this: a coding error — duplication, wrong specificity, a class-level entry where a drug-level one belonged — doesn't just risk a missed alert. It can just as easily produce an alert that's technically defensible but clinically useless: firing on a drug the patient is already stably taking, firing twice for the same reason, firing on a theoretical interaction so mild it's never actually acted on. Each of these individually seems minor. Accumulated across a shift, they teach a clinician that alerts from this system are noise, and noise gets clicked through — including, eventually, the one alert in a hundred that was catching something real.

This is why coding data quality belongs inside a patient-safety audit and not just a documentation-integrity one: **bad data doesn't only cause silence, it manufactures the noise that causes the next real alert to be ignored.**

contentSections.question: A unit's alert-override rate climbs steadily over six months with no change to the alert rules themselves. What's a coding-data explanation worth checking before assuming clinician attitudes have shifted?
contentSections.answer: Whether the volume of duplicate or overly-broad coded entries feeding that alert has grown over the same period — a new interface, a new intake process, or an EHR migration can quietly increase how often near-duplicate or class-level codes get created, which raises false-positive firing rate even though the rule itself never changed.
contentSections.hint: The rule is constant. What upstream data-generating process could have changed instead?

contentSections.body: A coding error that produces a spurious or duplicate alert is not a lesser problem than one that suppresses a needed alert — it degrades the same trust, from the other direction.

contentSections.title: Reading an alert-override pattern like a reviewer

contentSections.body: A quality team hands you an override report: one specific drug-interaction alert has a 94% override rate across the unit. The easy read is "clinicians are ignoring safety alerts." The harder, more useful read asks what's actually firing that often.

contentSections.scenario: Digging into the 94%-override alert, you find it fires whenever a patient's med list contains any drug coded to the broad RxNorm ingredient class "NSAID" and any drug in the class "anticoagulant" — including combinations that are, in practice, routinely and safely co-prescribed with monitoring, and including several low-dose topical NSAID formulations that carry negligible systemic interaction risk.
contentSections.question: What's the actual root cause of the 94% override rate?

options.label: Clinicians on this unit are unusually cavalier about drug interactions
The alert's coding is set at a class level too coarse to distinguish genuinely risky combinations from routine, monitored, or low-risk ones
The alert threshold needs to be raised so it fires less often overall

feedback.clinicians: This is the conclusion the raw override number invites, and it's usually wrong. A 94% override rate on one specific alert, on one unit, with clinicians who override plenty of *other* alerts at normal rates, points at something specific to that alert — not at a general attitude problem.
feedback.coarse: Right. When an alert fires on a class rather than the specific drug pair that's actually risky, it catches every low-risk and monitored combination along with the genuinely dangerous ones. Clinicians learn, correctly, that this particular alert is usually a false positive for their patient population, and override it as a matter of course — which is a rational response to a badly specified rule, not a discipline problem.
feedback.threshold: Raising a threshold (say, requiring a higher combined risk score) might reduce firing rate, but it doesn't fix the actual defect, which is that the rule is keyed to a coding level too coarse to distinguish real risk from routine care. A threshold change on a coarse rule just changes *how much* of the noise gets through, not whether the underlying logic is right.

contentSections.mechanism: **A high override rate is a symptom with several different possible causes, and "clinician complacency" is the least useful one to reach for first**, because it's the one that suggests no system change. The more productive question for an auditor: what is this alert actually keyed to — a specific drug pair, a drug class, a lab value range — and does that level of specificity match the level at which the real risk actually lives? Fixing the coding specificity of the alert's trigger condition, in this case moving from class-level to a curated list of the pairs with genuine, actionable risk, is very often the actual intervention, not clinician retraining.

contentSections.body: A high alert-override rate is evidence about the alert's specificity before it's evidence about clinician behavior. Trace what the alert is actually coded to fire on before assigning blame.

title: Where a wrong code stops being recoverable
description: Every chain has a point past which a wrong code stops being a documentation problem and becomes an outcome — and that point is rarely where it feels like it should be.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a chain of events to identify the specific point past which the error was no longer recoverable
Distinguish a recoverable near-miss from an unrecoverable harm event using the same chain framework

contentSections.body: Two charts, same underlying coding defect, two completely different endings. In one, a nurse double-checks a dose against the label before administering and catches it. In the other, the medication is already infusing before anyone notices. The code was equally wrong in both. What differed was where the chain ran out of exits.

contentSections.question: A wrong penicillin-allergy code (should be a mild childhood rash, coded as anaphylaxis) travels through a chain toward an alternative antibiotic being ordered instead of first-line penicillin. Put these checkpoints in the order they occur, earliest first — and identify, as you go, which is the last one that still counts as "recoverable."
steps: Allergy coded from an old note during chart abstraction
Code appears on the active allergy list, visible at every future encounter
Clinician orders an antibiotic; decision support blocks penicillin and suggests an alternative
Clinician accepts the alternative without querying the allergy's basis
Pharmacy verifies and dispenses the alternative
Alternative antibiotic is administered; patient has a bad reaction to the *alternative* drug, one they would not have had to penicillin
contentSections.explanation: Every checkpoint through pharmacy dispensing is still, in principle, recoverable — someone could still ask "how severe was this reaction, really?" and correct the record before a drug is chosen on its basis. The moment the alternative is administered, the chain has produced an outcome that can't be undone; nothing downstream can un-administer a drug. The clinician accepting the substitution without querying it is the last realistic human checkpoint — not because they did anything wrong by trusting a documented allergy, but because it's the last point where a two-sentence question ("how bad was this reaction, and to what?") would have changed what happened next. Everything before that point is about how the wrong code was created and carried; everything at and after that point is about whether harm was survivable.

contentSections.body: The last recoverable point in a chain is not always right before the harm. It's the last point where a specific, realistic question or check would have changed the outcome — and it's often several steps earlier than it looks.
Two coding errors, structurally identical, get filed completely differently by an audit team — correctly, but for a reason worth being explicit about.

contentSections.scenario: **Case A:** the same allergy-severity coding defect from the sequencing exercise is caught by a sharp-eyed pharmacist during verification, one step before dispensing. No alternative drug is ever given; the record gets corrected on the spot. **Case B:** identical defect, but pharmacy verification is skipped due to a system outage, and the patient receives the substituted drug and has a reaction to it.
contentSections.question: From a patient-safety-audit standpoint, should Case A and Case B be treated as the same severity of finding?

options.label: Yes — the underlying coding defect was identical, so the finding severity should be identical
No — Case B caused actual harm and Case A didn't, so B is strictly more severe and gets the higher rating
Both need reporting and root-cause tracing, but with different severity ratings — and Case A deserves just as much attention to *why the recovery worked*, not just that it did

feedback.same: Treating them as identical findings would be right if you were only grading the coding defect in isolation — but an audit exists to protect patients, and a near-miss that was caught is a genuinely different, less urgent event than one that wasn't. Equal severity ratings would blur that distinction in a way that misallocates urgency.
feedback.harm_only: This gets the severity ranking right but stops short of the more useful move: Case A isn't just "a lesser version of Case B," it's evidence about what recovery mechanism actually worked, which you want to strengthen and rely on less by luck next time.
feedback.both: Right on both counts. Case B is more severe because harm actually occurred — severity ratings have to track outcome, not just root cause, or a report loses the ability to triage. But Case A is not nothing: it's a near-miss with the exact same origin defect, and the fact that a pharmacist happened to catch it is worth investigating on its own — was that catch a reliable, designed-in check, or did it depend on one specific person's attention on one specific day? That question is what separates a system you can trust from a system that's gotten lucky so far.

contentSections.concept: **Severity tracks outcome; root-cause analysis tracks mechanism — and a rigorous audit runs both, on every case, including the ones where nothing bad happened.** The instinct to under-investigate near-misses is one of the most consistent gaps in real safety programs: harm gets full root-cause treatment because it's visible and demands an answer, while a near-miss with an identical origin gets a shrug because "it worked out." Every near-miss you don't trace is a harm event you're choosing to wait for instead.

contentSections.question: If your audit only had time to trace one of the two cases fully this week — the caught near-miss or the harm event — which should get the deeper root-cause trace, and why might that answer feel counterintuitive?
contentSections.answer: The harm event still needs the deeper trace, because it demonstrates the recovery mechanism failed outright and there's a confirmed injury to account for — but the counterintuitive part is how close the two traces should be in depth. If the near-miss trace gets rushed just because nothing went wrong, you never learn whether its "catch" was a reliable system feature you can lean on again.
contentSections.hint: This isn't really an either/or question — it's testing whether you'd let outcome alone determine how much investigative effort a case gets.

contentSections.body: A caught error and an uncaught one can share an identical origin. Rate them by outcome, but trace both by mechanism — a near-miss is free information about your system's real safety margin.

title: Practice — Trace Eight Coding Errors to Their Clinical Consequence
description: Eight scenarios, no new concepts: for each, identify the origin link, the recovery point that mattered, and whether it landed as a near-miss or a harm event.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the five-link chain framework to novel scenarios under time pressure

contentSections.body: No new ideas in this set — just reps. Each drill gives you a chain; find the origin, the last real exit, and what actually happened. Do them in one sitting if you can, or in pairs across two sessions if that's what today allows.
Eight different chains, one recurring move: find where the wrong fact was created, not just where it finally hurt someone.

title: Lab — Trace a Real Error to Every Downstream System It Touched
description: Take one coding error and build a trace diagram naming every system it passed through and the earliest point it could have been intercepted.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a complete trace diagram for a real or realistic coding error, naming every downstream system it reached

contentSections.body: Pick a coding error you've actually seen — in your own work, in a case a colleague described, or in your organization's incident log, with identifying details stripped. If you genuinely can't source a real one, use one of the two anonymized cases in the brief below. Either way, the deliverable is the same: a full trace, not a summary.

contentSections.title: Trace a Real Error to Every Downstream System It Touched
contentSections.brief: You've been asked to produce a trace diagram for a coding error — real, from your own experience or org's records (anonymized), or one of the two provided cases — that shows every system the error passed through and marks the earliest point interception was realistically possible. This is the artefact a safety committee would actually want to see: not "a mistake happened," but the specific mechanical path it took.
contentSections.deliverable: A trace diagram (can be a labeled flowchart, a table, or a written step-by-step — format is yours) naming: the origin link, every system/field/rule that read or propagated the error, the earliest realistic interception point, and what actually happened (near-miss or harm, with severity).

stages.title: Stage 1 — Pick and describe the case
stages.instructions: Write 4-6 sentences describing the error as it actually happened (or, if using a provided case: **Case A** — a diabetes A1c target coded from an outdated protocol version persists after the patient's care plan changes, and a newer, tighter target never gets applied to a subsequent dosing decision; **Case B** — a coded 'penicillin allergy: severe' turns out, on later query, to have been a single episode of mild nausea, and blocks first-line treatment for an unrelated infection two years later. Name who the affected systems and people are, without using real patient identifiers.
stages.checkpoint: You have a one-paragraph case description with no identifying details, ready to trace.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Map every link the error passed through
stages.instructions: List every system, field, or role the wrong code touched, in order: where it was created, where it was stored/displayed, what decision-support or workflow logic read it, who saw it and what they did. For each link, note in one sentence what that link did with the information it received — propagate unchanged, transform it, or act on it.
stages.checkpoint: You have an ordered list of every link, each with a one-sentence note on what it did.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Mark the earliest realistic interception point and the outcome
stages.instructions: Go back through your list and mark the single earliest point where a specific, realistic check or question would have caught the error — not the most convenient point in hindsight, the earliest one that was actually achievable given what that link could reasonably have known. State the actual outcome (near-miss or harm, and its severity) and whether the case, as it happened, caught it at that earliest point or later.
stages.checkpoint: Your trace names one specific earliest-interception link, with a stated reason it was realistic there and not earlier.

rubric.criterion: Origin correctly identified
rubric.meets: The trace names the actual point the wrong fact was first created or entered, not just the point it was first noticed.

rubric.criterion: Every link accounted for
rubric.meets: No system, field, or role that touched the code is skipped — including ones that only displayed it, noted as non-actionable rather than omitted.

rubric.criterion: Interception point is realistic, not hindsight-convenient
rubric.meets: The marked earliest interception point is justified by what that link could actually have known or checked at the time, not by what's obvious now.

rubric.criterion: Outcome and severity stated plainly
rubric.meets: The trace says clearly what actually happened (or would have happened) and rates it as near-miss or harm with a severity, not left implicit.

rubric.criterion: No patient-identifying details
rubric.meets: Ages, exact dates, facility names, or any other identifying detail are generalized or removed.

contentSections.body: A trace diagram is the artefact this whole module has been building toward: not a story about a mistake, but a mechanical map of exactly how it traveled and where it could have stopped.

title: Checkpoint — How Coding Errors Reach Patients
description: Ungraded retrieval on the chain framework from this module — first module in the phase, so all ten questions draw from what you just covered.

learningObjectives.text: Recall the five-link chain and the origin/recovery-point distinction under low-stakes retrieval conditions

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — How Coding Errors Reach Patients
contentSections.framing: Ten questions, nothing graded, no timer. This is the first module of the phase, so everything here pulls from what you just covered — later checkpoints will start reaching back further.

questions.prompt: In the five-link chain, what comes between "the record" and "the clinician"?

options.label: Decision support
The patient
Billing

questions.explanation: The order is code → record → decision support → clinician → patient. Decision support is the rules layer that reads the record before a clinician ever sees an alert.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between the "origin" link and a "recovery" link in a chain?

options.label: The origin is where the wrong fact was created; a recovery link is any later point that could have caught it
They're the same thing, described two ways
The origin is always the clinician

questions.explanation: The origin is a single point — where the wrong fact entered. Recovery links are every later checkpoint that had, and possibly missed, a chance to catch it.

questions.prompt: Why do problem lists tend to accumulate stale entries rather than staying curated?

options.label: Adding a problem is a normal part of a visit; removing one requires a separate, unrewarded action nobody's workflow asks for
EHR software doesn't allow deleting problems
Clinicians are required to keep every historical diagnosis coded as active

questions.explanation: Nothing in ordinary workflow removes an entry, only adds one — resolving a stale problem takes deliberate, unrewarded effort.

questions.prompt: A stale diagnosis code sits on a problem list. Which kind of downstream system is most likely to silently act on it as if it were current?

options.label: The after-visit summary printer
A risk-adjustment or screening-suppression tool that scores or triages off coded diagnoses
Neither — problem list entries are purely documentation

questions.explanation: Anything that scores, screens, or triages off the problem list inherits stale entries as if they were true today. Display-only surfaces like a printed summary don't feed any decision.

questions.prompt: Why is allergy and medication data riskier, in immediate terms, than most other coded fields?

options.label: It has the shortest line to an order changing within the same encounter, sometimes the same hour
It's coded less accurately than other fields on average
It's the only field decision support reads at all

questions.explanation: A problem-list error can sit inert for years; an allergy or medication error can change what a clinician orders within the same visit.

questions.prompt: A discharge note says a patient "gets nauseated with codeine, tolerates other opioids fine," and it gets coded as a class-level opiate allergy. What's the core defect?

options.label: A single-drug intolerance was generalized to an entire drug class, contradicting what the source note actually said
Codeine isn't actually an opiate
The severity wasn't marked high enough

questions.explanation: The note explicitly said other opioids are tolerated — that's the clinical content, and it's exactly what got lost in the generalization to a class-level entry.

questions.prompt: A specific drug-interaction alert has a 94% override rate on one unit. What should an auditor check first?

options.label: Whether clinicians on that unit are generally careless with alerts
What level of specificity the alert is actually keyed to — a specific drug pair, or a broad class that catches routine, low-risk combinations too
Whether the alert threshold is simply set too low across the whole system

questions.explanation: A coarse, class-level trigger catches routine and monitored combinations along with genuinely risky ones, training clinicians to override it as a rational response — not a discipline problem.

questions.prompt: How can a coding error cause harm through noise rather than silence?

options.label: It can't — coding errors only ever suppress alerts that should have fired
A duplicate or overly broad entry can cause spurious or repeated alerts, training clinicians to expect noise and click through — including, eventually, a real one
Noise only affects billing, never patient safety

questions.explanation: Bad data doesn't only cause silence — it can manufacture false-positive noise that erodes trust in the alert system generally, which is its own path to a missed real alert later.

questions.prompt: In the penicillin-allergy chain example, what made the clinician's acceptance of the substituted antibiotic the "last realistic checkpoint," rather than an earlier or later one?

options.label: It was the last point where a brief, realistic question would still have changed what happened next — everything after was outcome, not prevention
It was simply the point closest in time to the harm
Clinicians are always the last checkpoint in every chain by definition

questions.explanation: The last realistic checkpoint isn't defined by proximity to the harm — it's the last point where a specific, achievable action would have changed the outcome. Here, that was one short question about the allergy's actual basis.

questions.prompt: Two identical coding defects — one caught by a pharmacist before dispensing, one not caught, causing harm. How should an audit treat the caught one?

options.label: As a non-event, since no harm occurred
As a near-miss worth its own root-cause trace — including asking whether the catch was a reliable, designed-in check or just luck on one person's attentive day
As equally severe as the harm event, since the underlying defect was identical

questions.explanation: Severity tracks outcome (so the near-miss is rated lower), but root-cause tracing should run on both — an uninvestigated near-miss is a harm event you're choosing to wait for.

contentSections.body: The chain framework — origin, links, recovery point, outcome — is the lens the rest of this phase builds on. If any of these felt shaky, that's useful information, not a failing grade.

title: Scoping an audit so it can actually be finished
description: An audit with no scope tries to check everything and finishes nothing. Scoping is the first safety decision you make, before you've looked at a single chart.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a workable audit scope from one that will never finish
Choose a scoping boundary that still captures the highest-risk area of a system

contentSections.body: "Audit the accuracy of our AI-assisted coding" is not a scope. It's a mission statement. Six months later the team has looked at a little of everything and can defend none of it, because nothing was ever bounded enough to actually complete.

contentSections.scenario: A health system's compliance lead asks you to "audit the coding tool's accuracy across the hospital." You have three weeks and one other reviewer.
contentSections.question: What's the first scoping move that makes this actually finishable?

options.label: Pick a narrow slice — one service line, one code type, one time window — and go deep
Sample a small number of charts from every service line for broad coverage
Start immediately and narrow the scope later once you see what's out there

feedback.narrow: Right. A narrow, deep scope — say, allergy and medication coding accuracy in the emergency department over the last quarter — produces findings you can actually defend, because you've looked hard enough at a bounded population to say something true about it. "A little of everything" produces findings that are true of nothing in particular.
feedback.broad: Broad-and-shallow feels like coverage, but it produces a report that says "we found a few issues everywhere," which tells nobody what to fix first. It also multiplies your context-switching cost — every service line has different documentation conventions, and three weeks isn't enough to learn all of them.
feedback.start: Narrowing later sounds efficient but almost never happens under a deadline — once the team is three days in and has looked at whatever charts were easiest to pull, that becomes the de facto scope by accident, unexamined and unjustified, instead of a scope chosen on purpose for the highest risk.

contentSections.concept: **Scope is a resource-allocation decision, made explicitly, before the work starts** — not a byproduct of what turned out to be convenient to pull. A scope chosen on purpose can be defended in the report's first paragraph: "we chose X because of Y." A scope that accreted by accident can't be defended at all, because nobody decided it.

contentSections.body:
A workable scope answers three questions in one or two sentences each, before any chart gets pulled:

1. **What population** — which service, which code type, which time window. Specific enough that someone else could pull the same sample.
2. **What question** — accuracy of a specific field, not "quality" in general. "Is allergy severity coded correctly" is answerable. "Is our coding good" is not.
3. **What would make this worth doing** — the risk hypothesis. Why this population, this field, right now? "Because the ED has the highest-acuity, fastest-turnaround documentation, and allergy fields feed same-visit decision support" is a defensible reason. "Because it hadn't been looked at yet" is not, on its own — there's always something that hasn't been looked at yet.

contentSections.question: Two proposed scopes for the same three weeks: (A) allergy coding accuracy, ED only, last quarter; (B) all coding accuracy, hospital-wide, last year. Which one is more likely to survive a challenge from a skeptical department head asking "how do you know this is representative?"
contentSections.answer: (A). A narrow, explicitly bounded scope can honestly say what it covers and what it doesn't — "this is ED allergy coding, last quarter; we make no claim about other departments or fields." A broad scope with the same three weeks of effort spread thin can't make that same honest, bounded claim about any of its sub-areas, which is exactly what a skeptical challenge will expose.
contentSections.hint: "Representative" is a claim about depth within a defined boundary, not about how much ground you covered.

contentSections.body: A defensible scope names its population, its question, and its reason, before a single chart is pulled. If you can't state those three things in two sentences, the scope isn't ready.

contentSections.title: Choosing where the risk actually is

contentSections.body: Given a free choice of scope, there's a strong pull toward auditing what's easiest to check — structured fields with clean audit trails — rather than what's riskiest. Those are rarely the same area.

contentSections.scenario: Across health systems that have run formal AI-assisted-coding safety audits, a recurring finding is that the highest concentration of clinically significant coding errors doesn't sit in the highest-volume code category.
contentSections.question: Roughly what fraction of a system's total coded fields typically account for the majority of coding errors serious enough to reach a decision-support system or an alert?
contentSections.explanation: It's a lopsided distribution in most systems that have actually measured it — a relatively small share of field types (allergy/medication data, a handful of high-stakes diagnosis codes, a few frequently-miscoded procedure distinctions) account for a disproportionate majority of the errors that matter clinically. The reason to know this isn't the exact number, it's the shape: scoping by volume ("audit the code type we assign most often") and scoping by risk ("audit the code types that feed the riskiest downstream decisions") point at different populations, and the second one is almost always the better use of three weeks.

contentSections.body: A useful scoping heuristic: rank candidate areas not by how often they're coded, but by how directly and quickly a wrong code in that area could change a clinical decision — using the chain framework from the last module. Allergy and medication data ranks high because the chain from code to decision to patient is short. A rarely-updated demographic field ranks low even if it's technically wrong often, because nothing downstream acts on it quickly. Scope toward the short chains first.
Scope by how fast a wrong code could reach a decision, not by how often that field gets coded. The two rankings usually disagree, and the risk ranking should win.

title: Sampling for harm, not for reassurance
description: A random sample tells you the average error rate. A sample built to find harm tells you where the dangerous errors actually cluster — and those require different sampling strategies.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a purely random sample under-represents the highest-risk cases
Design a stratified sample that deliberately over-weights high-risk cases

contentSections.title: What a random sample is actually good for

contentSections.body: A random sample of 100 charts finds a 4% coding error rate. That's a real, defensible number — and it's also almost useless for finding the one error type that could actually hurt someone, because that error type might occur in 0.5% of charts and never show up in a sample of 100 at all.

contentSections.scenario: A team draws a purely random sample of 150 charts across an entire hospital to check coding accuracy. The audit reports a 3.2% overall error rate and concludes the system is performing well. Three months later, a cluster of severe allergy-coding errors in the oncology unit — a low-volume, high-risk area — comes to light through an unrelated incident report.
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism that let the random sample miss this?

options.label: The sample size was too small overall
Oncology is a low-volume unit, so random sampling proportional to volume drew almost none of its charts, even though its risk per chart was high
The auditors weren't looking for allergy errors specifically

feedback.size: A bigger random sample would help somewhat, but the core problem isn't size — it's that random sampling draws charts in proportion to volume, and a low-volume, high-risk unit will always be underrepresented relative to its actual danger, no matter how large the random sample gets.
feedback.proportional: Right. Pure random sampling is proportional to volume by construction — a unit that generates 2% of total charts will get roughly 2% of the sample, regardless of how dangerous its errors are per chart. A rare, high-severity error cluster in a low-volume area can sit below a random sample's detection floor indefinitely.
feedback.specific: The audit's stated scope was general accuracy, not allergy-specific — so this isn't really about what they were looking for, it's about which charts they ever looked at in the first place. A chart from the affected unit that was never sampled couldn't reveal anything, regardless of what the auditors would have noticed if they'd seen it.

contentSections.mechanism: **Random sampling answers "what's the average error rate," and stratified sampling answers "where are the dangerous errors."** They are different questions requiring different designs, and a patient-safety audit almost always needs the second one, sometimes alongside the first. Confusing the two is one of the most common ways an audit produces a clean-looking report that misses exactly the thing it existed to catch.

contentSections.body: **Stratifying for harm** means deliberately over-sampling the populations most likely to produce serious errors, even though that makes the sample no longer statistically representative of the whole system. That's a fair trade in a safety audit: you are not trying to publish an unbiased estimate of average performance, you are trying to find the errors that could hurt someone. Concretely: pull disproportionately from high-acuity units, from fields with short chains to a decision (allergy, medication, dosing-relevant diagnoses), and from any area with a known prior incident, near-miss report, or high alert-override rate — then say plainly in the report that the sample was risk-weighted, not representative, so nobody misreads your findings as a system-wide rate.
A random sample tells you the average. A risk-stratified sample tells you where the dangerous cases live. A safety audit needs the second one and should say clearly which one it ran.
Stratifying sounds abstract until you actually have to write down the strata and a number for each one.

contentSections.question: Put these steps of building a risk-stratified sample in the order you'd actually do them.
steps: List the candidate strata: units, code types, or fields ranked by chain-length-to-decision from the previous lesson
Decide a target number of charts per stratum, weighted toward the highest-risk strata rather than equal or volume-proportional
Pull the actual charts within each stratum, using a random draw within that stratum to avoid cherry-picking
Document the stratification logic in the audit's methods section before reviewing a single chart
contentSections.explanation: The order matters because documenting the logic before reviewing anything is what makes the sample defensible later — if you decide your strata after seeing which charts look interesting, you've built a sample that confirms what you already suspected rather than one that tests it. Random draw *within* a stratum still matters even though the stratum itself was chosen for risk: you don't want to also hand-pick which specific charts inside oncology get reviewed, or you've reintroduced the same bias one level down.

contentSections.body: Choose and document strata before you look at any chart. Then randomize within each stratum. Both halves matter — risk-weighting the strata and randomizing inside them.

title: Severity classification that people agree on
description: A severity scale that two reviewers apply differently to the same finding isn't a severity scale, it's a coin flip with extra steps.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a severity scale's categories are concrete enough to produce agreement between independent reviewers
Apply a severity classification consistently to a set of findings with differing outcomes and differing likelihoods

contentSections.body: Two reviewers, same finding, same scale — "Low / Medium / High / Critical" — and one calls it Medium, the other calls it Critical. Neither is wrong by the scale's own words, because the scale's words don't actually constrain the choice.

contentSections.code:
Severity Scale (as written in the audit team's guide):

  Low      — minor issue, limited impact
  Medium   — moderate issue, some impact
  High     — significant issue, considerable impact
  Critical — severe issue, major impact
contentSections.question: What's wrong with this scale?

options.label: It only has four levels; it needs more granularity
Every category is defined using a word from the category name itself, giving a reviewer nothing concrete to anchor a decision to
It doesn't mention regulatory categories

feedback.levels: Adding more levels to a circularly-defined scale just gives reviewers more categories to disagree about in exactly the same way — the problem isn't granularity, it's that none of the categories are anchored to anything concrete.
feedback.circular: Right. "Significant issue, considerable impact" for High and "severe issue, major impact" for Critical are using near-synonyms of the category name to define the category — a reviewer gets no actual guidance about what fact pattern belongs where. Two reasonable people will read "considerable" differently every time.
feedback.reg: Regulatory categories might be worth cross-referencing eventually, but their absence isn't why two reviewers disagree on the same finding today — that's a definitional problem, not a completeness problem.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A severity scale is only doing its job if it lets two independent reviewers, looking at the same finding, land on the same category *without discussing it first*. That requires each category to be anchored to a concrete, observable fact — not a synonym of severity. A workable version replaces adjectives with facts: **Critical** — reached the patient and caused or could plausibly have caused permanent harm or death; **High** — reached the patient with reversible harm, or was a near-miss one step from irreversible harm; **Medium** — reached the patient with no clinical effect, or a near-miss caught two or more steps before harm; **Low** — never reached a point where it could affect a clinical decision. Every level is now a testable claim about what actually happened, not a vibe.

contentSections.body: The anchoring facts worth building a scale around, based on this phase's chain framework, are: **did it reach the patient**, **was the harm reversible**, and **how many recoverable steps away from harm was it caught**. Any two reviewers who agree on those three facts about a case will land on the same severity, which is the entire point — the scale should make disagreement about the *facts* possible (reasonable people can dispute whether harm was truly reversible) while making disagreement about the *category*, given agreed facts, nearly impossible.
A severity scale defined by synonyms produces disagreement. A severity scale anchored to observable facts — reached the patient, reversible, how many steps from harm — produces agreement.
The anchored scale still has to handle the case that doesn't cleanly fit — the one where reasonable people genuinely can dispute a fact, not just a category.

contentSections.title: Rating a genuinely ambiguous finding
contentSections.opening: A coded medication mapping error is caught by a pharmacist during verification, before dispensing — clearly a near-miss, not a harm event. But the pharmacist herself says in a follow-up interview that she "almost missed it, and only caught it because I happened to double-check that particular class today, not as part of the standard workflow."

rate.situation: Using the anchored scale, this is a near-miss caught before harm — by the facts, that alone would put it at Medium (reached the patient with no clinical effect... but wait, it never reached the patient at all, so arguably Low). But the pharmacist's comment suggests the catch was closer to luck than the facts alone capture.
rate.question: How do you rate it?

choices.label: Rate it Low, strictly by the facts — no harm, didn't even reach a near-miss decision point
choices.consequence: The severity rating is technically defensible but the report loses the information that this was a near-luck catch, which is exactly the kind of finding that should drive urgency toward fixing the underlying process, not just noting it.

choices.label: Rate it High to reflect how close it actually came
choices.consequence: This breaks the scale's whole purpose — if severity ratings start absorbing subjective 'how lucky did we get' judgments, two reviewers will diverge on identical facts again, which is the exact problem the anchored scale was built to prevent.

choices.label: Rate it Low by the anchored facts, and separately flag it for root-cause escalation with the pharmacist's comment quoted directly
choices.consequence: The severity rating stays clean and comparable across the whole audit, and the near-luck element is preserved and acted on through a different channel — root-cause priority — instead of being smuggled into the severity number.

buried.summary: Technically correct, but the report reads as if this finding needs no urgency, when the interview transcript says otherwise.
buried.lesson: A severity scale that can't express "technically low-severity but structurally lucky" isn't broken — it just needs a second channel for that information. The fix isn't bending severity, it's adding a companion field.

broken.summary: The severity scale now means something different for this finding than for every other Low-rated near-miss in the report, and nobody reading the report can tell which is which.
broken.lesson: Bending a category to capture urgency destroys the one property that makes a severity scale useful — comparability across findings. It also sets a precedent: the next reviewer, facing a similarly close call, has no way to know whether 'High' means 'reached the patient' or 'felt scary.'

resolved.summary: The audit report shows a clean, comparable severity rating and a separate, specific root-cause priority flag with the reason quoted.
resolved.lesson: Severity and urgency are two different axes. A rigorous audit keeps them separate and lets each do its own job — severity says what happened, a root-cause priority flag says how much this deserves attention regardless of what happened.

contentSections.body: When a finding's severity and its underlying urgency pull in different directions, don't bend the severity category to capture urgency — rate severity by the facts, and flag urgency separately.

title: Evidence: what you must keep for every finding
description: A finding without preserved evidence is a claim, and claims get argued with. Evidence is what turns a finding into something a skeptic can check for themselves.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the minimum evidence set a finding needs to survive a challenge
Evaluate whether a piece of evidence would actually hold up if the underlying system changed before the report was read

contentSections.body: A finding says a coding tool mismapped a drug name. Two months later, the vendor pushes an update, the specific mapping table changes, and the finding can no longer be reproduced by anyone trying to verify it — including you.

contentSections.scenario: You're finalizing a finding about a mismapped drug name discovered during your audit sample. Consider what to actually preserve, as opposed to just describe from memory in the write-up.
contentSections.question: Which of these are things you should capture and keep, not just summarize?

items.label: A screenshot or export of the actual chart entry showing the wrong mapping, timestamped
The raw source text the mapping was derived from, exactly as it appeared
Your own one-sentence paraphrase of what the note said
The version or date of the coding tool / mapping table in use at the time
Which reviewer found it and when, for chain-of-custody if the finding is later disputed

explanation.screenshot: Yes — a preserved, timestamped capture of the actual entry is the thing that survives the underlying system changing. A description of it does not.
explanation.raw_note: Yes — your interpretation of a note can be challenged; the raw text itself is much harder to argue with, and it's what lets someone else independently check your read of it.
explanation.your_summary: No — a paraphrase is useful in the write-up for readability, but it cannot substitute for the underlying evidence, because a paraphrase can drift from the source in ways nobody, including you months later, would catch.
explanation.system_version: Yes — without this, a finding about a specific mapping error becomes unverifiable the moment the vendor updates the table, because nobody can tell whether you're describing the current system or an old one.
explanation.reviewer_id: Yes — if a finding is challenged, being able to say precisely who found it, when, and under what sampling stratum is what lets the audit withstand scrutiny rather than relying on collective memory.

contentSections.synthesis: The test for whether something counts as evidence, versus just narrative: **would it still prove the finding if the underlying system changed tomorrow and nobody remembered the details?** A screenshot survives that test. A paraphrase doesn't.

contentSections.body: Evidence is whatever would still prove your finding if the system changed and everyone's memory of the details faded. Capture that, not a summary of it.

Preserving evidence and protecting patient privacy pull in the same direction more often than people expect — the discipline that makes evidence rigorous is largely the same discipline that keeps it minimal.

contentSections.question: You're capturing evidence for a finding and the fastest way to grab a clean screenshot also captures the patient's full name and MRN in the header. What's the actual fix, versus the tempting shortcut of just being careful with who sees the file afterward?
contentSections.answer: Redact or crop the identifying header before saving, and reference the case by an internal audit ID that maps back to the chart only through a separate, access-controlled log — not "be careful who sees the file," which depends on every future person handling it correctly and never fails safely if it doesn't.
contentSections.hint: Controlling who *can* see something is weaker than never capturing more than you need in the first place.

contentSections.body: Every piece of evidence you preserve should carry the minimum patient-identifying detail needed to prove the point, and no more — this is the same **minimum necessary** principle that governs clinical data access generally, applied to your own audit trail. A screenshot of a mismapped drug name doesn't need the patient's full name and date of birth visible in frame; a case identifier that only your audit team can trace back to the chart, kept in a separate access-controlled log, does the same evidentiary job with far less exposure. An audit that leaves unredacted patient identifiers scattered across screenshots in a shared drive is a second safety problem stacked on top of whatever it's investigating.

Preserve the minimum patient detail that proves the finding, referenced through a separate access-controlled log — not because privacy rules require it in the abstract, but because an audit trail full of unredacted identifiers is a risk you created on top of the one you're investigating.

title: Auditing at variable capacity, in stages
description: A 50-minute audit session assumes a 50-minute good stretch that not every reviewer has every day. Staging the work is not a compromise on rigor — done right, it improves it.

learningObjectives.text: Design an audit workflow broken into independently resumable stages

contentSections.title: Why staging helps rigor, not just accessibility

contentSections.body: The instinct is to treat staged, interruptible audit work as a concession — something you do because not everyone can sit for an unbroken hour. It's worth noticing it also produces better audits, for everyone, independent of capacity.

contentSections.scenario: Compare two ways of reviewing a 12-chart sample: (A) one reviewer works through all 12 in a single sitting, applying the severity scale as they go; (B) the same reviewer reads and scopes all 12 in one sitting, then rates severity for all 12 in a separate, later sitting, using only the preserved evidence — not memory of how the chart "felt" while reading it.
contentSections.question: Which approach is more resistant to a specific, well-documented bias in this kind of work?

options.label: A — momentum keeps context fresh
B — separating the reading stage from the rating stage reduces the chance that an emotionally vivid early chart skews how later charts in the same session get rated
Neither — severity should be rated immediately or not at all

feedback.a: Momentum has a real cost here: a reviewer who rates severity chart-by-chart in one long sitting is vulnerable to anchoring — a genuinely severe early finding can make a moderate later one look mild by comparison, or fatigue late in the session can flatten everything toward the same rating.
feedback.b: Right, and this is the useful discovery: staging isn't just accommodation, it's a structural defense against contrast and fatigue effects. Rating all 12 findings together, from preserved evidence rather than in-the-moment impression, using the anchored facts-based scale from lesson 3, produces more consistent ratings than doing it one at a time in the heat of discovery.
feedback.neither: Delayed rating using preserved evidence is exactly what makes this work — the evidence-preservation habit from the last lesson is what makes it possible to rate accurately later rather than needing to rate in the moment at all.

contentSections.concept: **A staged workflow — read and preserve evidence in one pass, rate severity in a separate pass, write findings in a third — isn't a lesser version of doing it all at once. It's a better version**, because it breaks the process at exactly the points where continuous work introduces bias, and it happens to also be the version that fits into 20-minute blocks on a day that doesn't offer more than that.

contentSections.body:
A workable three-stage split for this module's lab, and for real audit work generally:

1. **Read and capture** — go through the sample, read source documentation, preserve evidence per lesson 4. No rating yet. Can be done in short blocks, any order.
2. **Rate** — using only the preserved evidence, apply the anchored severity scale to every finding in one focused pass, ideally close together in time so the scale is applied consistently. Lower energy cost per finding than reading, since the facts are already extracted.
3. **Write** — turn rated findings into the report format from the next module. This stage benefits from a rested state most, since it's where clarity of writing matters most.
Split reading, rating, and writing into separate passes. It's not a lesser method for a harder day — the separation itself reduces contrast bias and fatigue drift, on any day.
The gap between "I'll pick this up tomorrow" and actually picking it up tomorrow, correctly, is usually a documentation problem, not a willpower problem.

contentSections.intro: Build a minimal resume-state note for the audit-in-progress from lesson 1's scenario — you're partway through the read-and-capture stage, 7 of 12 sampled charts done.

fields.prompt: What must it record about exactly where you stopped?
options: Which specific chart IDs are done and which remain, by sample ID — not "about half"
A general sense of progress
Nothing — you'll remember
fields.correctValue: Which specific chart IDs are done and which remain, by sample ID — not "about half"
fields.feedback: Exact IDs, because "about half" forces you to re-derive exactly where you were, which is the whole cost staging is trying to avoid.

fields.prompt: What must it record about any partially-worked chart?
options: Whatever's been captured so far, explicitly marked incomplete — not silently left to look finished
Nothing, finish it fully or skip it entirely
Just a note to 'come back to this one'
fields.correctValue: Whatever's been captured so far, explicitly marked incomplete — not silently left to look finished
fields.feedback: An incomplete capture that isn't marked as incomplete is worse than no capture at all — a future you (or a teammate) will trust it as done and skip verifying it.

fields.prompt: What should it say about the very next action?
options: The specific next chart ID and what stage of the read-and-capture checklist to start at
"Continue the audit"
Nothing — the chart list makes it obvious
fields.correctValue: The specific next chart ID and what stage of the read-and-capture checklist to start at
fields.feedback: Naming the exact next action removes the highest-friction moment in resuming work: the few minutes of re-orienting that make people put it off another day.

contentSections.synthesis: A resume note isn't a summary of progress — it's a set of instructions precise enough that a tired version of you, or a colleague covering for you, could pick the work up cold in under two minutes.

contentSections.body: A staged audit only works if resuming is cheap. That means recording exact position, explicitly flagging anything partial, and naming the next concrete action — not a vague sense of where things stand.

title: Practice — Scope Seven Audits Under Real Constraints
description: Seven scoping and sampling scenarios, no new concepts — build the judgment for turning a vague ask into a finishable, risk-weighted audit.

learningObjectives.text: Apply scoping, stratified sampling, severity classification, and evidence standards to novel constrained scenarios

contentSections.body: Same drill format as last module: no new ideas, just reps applying scope, sample, severity, and evidence under time and resource constraints that won't always be generous.
Scoping judgment is built the same way sampling judgment is: by making the call under a real constraint and checking it against a defensible standard, over and over.

title: Lab — Run a Scoped Safety Audit End to End
description: Design and run a real, bounded audit: scope, method, sample, findings, severities, and evidence — the full cycle this module has been building toward.

learningObjectives.text: Design and execute a complete, bounded safety audit with defensible scope, sampling, severity ratings, and preserved evidence

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole arc in one deliverable. If you have access to real (anonymizable) records, use them at the scale this brief allows; if not, use the provided scenario. Either way, every stage produces something written, not just something decided in your head.

contentSections.title: Run a Scoped Safety Audit End to End
contentSections.brief: You've been given three weeks (compressed here into this lab) and told to audit AI-assisted coding accuracy somewhere in a health system.
