Scenario, if you don't have your own: a mid-size hospital's oncology and ED units both use the same AI-assisted coding tool for allergy, medication, and diagnosis fields; there's been one recent near-miss incident report from oncology involving a medication mapping error, and no prior formal audit of this tool. Produce a complete, bounded audit: scope statement, sampling method, a set of findings (real or realistically constructed) with severities, and a note on evidence handling.
contentSections.deliverable: A written audit package: (1) a scope statement naming population, question, and risk rationale; (2) a sampling method with strata and rationale; (3) at least 5 findings, each with a severity rating using the anchored facts-based scale; (4) a one-paragraph note on what evidence was preserved and how patient identifiers were minimized.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Scope and sampling design
stages.instructions: Write the scope statement (population, question, risk rationale) and the sampling method (strata, weighting, target counts per stratum) before reviewing anything. This mirrors lesson 1 and 2's exact sequence.
stages.checkpoint: You have a scope statement and sampling plan, written down, that could be handed to someone else to execute.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Review and capture evidence
stages.instructions: Work through your sample (real, or constructed realistically from the scenario) and capture evidence for each finding per lesson 4's standard — what would prove it, minimized to necessary patient detail.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least 5 findings with evidence captured, not yet rated.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Rate severity in a separate pass
stages.instructions: Using only the captured evidence, not memory of reviewing the chart, rate each finding's severity using the anchored scale from lesson 3. Do this as one focused pass across all findings, per lesson 5's staging principle.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a severity rating, justified by the anchored facts (reached patient / reversible / steps from harm).

stages.title: Stage 4 — Package it
stages.instructions: Assemble the scope statement, sampling method, rated findings, and evidence-handling note into one document, in that order.
stages.checkpoint: You have one document a safety committee could read start to finish without needing to ask a clarifying question about method.

rubric.criterion: Scope is bounded and justified
rubric.meets: Names a specific population, a specific question, and a stated risk rationale for why this scope over others.

rubric.criterion: Sampling is stratified for risk, not just random
rubric.meets: Strata are named and weighted toward higher-risk areas, with the weighting rationale stated, and randomization used within strata.

rubric.criterion: Severity ratings use the anchored scale consistently
rubric.meets: Every finding's severity is justified by the three anchoring facts, not by adjectives, and similar fact patterns get similar ratings.

rubric.criterion: Evidence standard is met and minimized
rubric.meets: The note states what was preserved (not just described) and how patient-identifying detail was kept to the minimum necessary.

rubric.criterion: Package is self-contained
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the process could follow scope through findings without needing to ask what method was used.

contentSections.body: This is the shape of a real safety audit: bounded on purpose, sampled for danger rather than comfort, rated by fact rather than feeling, and backed by evidence that survives being checked.

title: Checkpoint — Running a Safety Audit
description: Ungraded retrieval — second module of the phase, so all ten questions still draw from this module; later checkpoints will start reaching back.

learningObjectives.text: Recall the scoping, sampling, severity, and evidence standards from this module under low-stakes retrieval conditions

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Running a Safety Audit
contentSections.framing: Ten questions, nothing graded, no timer. Still module 2 of the phase, so this pulls entirely from what you just covered here.

questions.prompt: What are the three things a defensible audit scope must state before any chart is reviewed?

options.label: Population, question, and risk rationale
Budget, headcount, and deadline
The auditors' names and credentials

questions.explanation: A workable scope names what population it covers, what specific question it answers, and why that population and question were chosen over others — resource details and credentials don't make a scope defensible.

questions.prompt: Why is a broad, hospital-wide scope often worse than a narrow one under a tight deadline?

options.label: It spreads effort so thin that no sub-area gets a defensible, bounded finding
It's always illegal to audit more than one department at a time
Broad scopes are actually always better if time allows

questions.explanation: A broad-and-shallow audit produces findings that are true of nothing in particular — narrow-and-deep produces a claim you can actually stand behind for the area it covers.

questions.prompt: Why does pure random sampling tend to miss dangerous error clusters in low-volume, high-risk units?

options.label: Random sampling draws charts proportional to volume, so a low-volume unit is underrepresented regardless of how dangerous its errors are
Random sampling always excludes oncology and ED by design
It doesn't — random sampling always catches high-risk clusters eventually

questions.explanation: Volume-proportional sampling structurally underrepresents rare-but-severe clusters in low-volume areas — this is the exact mechanism a risk-stratified sample is built to correct.

questions.prompt: What's the correct order for building a risk-stratified sample?

options.label: Define and document strata and weighting first, then randomize the specific charts pulled within each stratum
Pull whichever charts look interesting, then explain the pattern afterward
Randomize everything, including which strata to use

questions.explanation: Documenting the stratification logic before reviewing anything is what makes the sample defensible; randomizing within each stratum (not hand-picking specific charts) avoids reintroducing bias at a lower level.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with a severity scale whose categories are "Low / Medium / High / Critical," each defined using a synonym of the category name?

options.label: It gives reviewers nothing concrete to anchor to, so independent reviewers will disagree on identical findings
It doesn't have enough categories
Nothing — this is a standard, workable scale

questions.explanation: Circular definitions (defining "High" as "significant") give no concrete guidance, so two reasonable reviewers reading the same finding can land on different categories.

questions.prompt: What three anchoring facts does a workable severity scale use instead of adjectives?

options.label: Whether it reached the patient, whether the harm was reversible, and how many recoverable steps it was caught from harm
How embarrassing the finding is, how senior the responsible clinician is, and how old the code is
The exact ICD-10-CM code involved, its character count, and its billing weight

questions.explanation: Anchoring to reached-patient, reversibility, and steps-from-harm gives independent reviewers the same concrete facts to check, producing consistent ratings.

questions.prompt: A near-miss is caught, but only by luck rather than a reliable process step. How should that "felt closer to harm than the facts suggest" information be handled?

options.label: Rate severity by the facts (a near-miss), and flag the near-luck element separately for root-cause priority — don't bend the severity category
Inflate the severity rating to reflect how close it felt
Omit the near-luck detail since severity is already decided

questions.explanation: Severity and urgency are different axes — bending severity to capture urgency destroys comparability across findings; a separate flag preserves both pieces of information cleanly.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether something counts as preserved "evidence" for a finding, versus just narrative description?

options.label: Whether it would still prove the finding if the underlying system changed and nobody remembered the details
Whether it's longer than two sentences
Whether a senior reviewer personally witnessed it

questions.explanation: A screenshot or raw source text survives a system update or a fading memory; a paraphrase does not — that durability is what makes something evidence rather than narrative.

questions.prompt: How should patient-identifying detail be handled when capturing audit evidence?

options.label: Minimized at capture time — redact what isn't needed and reference cases through a separate access-controlled log, rather than relying on careful handling afterward
Always captured in full for completeness, restricted only by who can view the file later
Never captured at all, even in redacted or referenced form

questions.explanation: Minimizing at the point of capture doesn't depend on every future person handling the file correctly — it fails safely, unlike a policy that only restricts viewing access after the fact.

questions.prompt: Why does splitting an audit into read-and-capture, rate, and write stages improve rigor, not just accessibility?

options.label: Rating findings together from preserved evidence, separately from reading, reduces contrast and fatigue effects that skew ratings done chart-by-chart in one sitting
It doesn't improve rigor — it's purely an accommodation with a rigor cost
It only helps because it takes less total time

questions.explanation: Rating in one focused pass, from preserved evidence rather than in-the-moment impression, avoids anchoring and fatigue drift — a structural benefit independent of who's doing the work or how much time they have in one sitting.

contentSections.body: Scope, stratify, rate by fact, preserve evidence, stage the work. Those five moves are the method this whole module built — the next module is about writing what they find.

title: The finding nobody could act on, and why
description: A technically accurate finding that names no owner, no reproduction, and no plain-language impact just moves the problem from your desk to someone else's backlog, unsolved.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose why a specific finding, though factually accurate, produced no action
Name the elements a finding needs regardless of audience

contentSections.title: Accurate and useless at the same time

contentSections.body: "Finding 14: ICD-10-CM specificity issue, oncology, moderate severity." Every word of that sentence is true. Six weeks later it's still open, because nobody — not the coder, not the engineer, not the clinical lead — knows what to actually do with it.

contentSections.code:
Finding 14 (as filed):

ISSUE: ICD-10-CM specificity issue
AREA: Oncology
SEVERITY: Moderate
DESCRIPTION: Several encounters show diagnosis codes
lacking appropriate specificity per documentation.
RECOMMENDATION: Improve coding specificity in oncology.
contentSections.question: Why has this finding sat unresolved for six weeks?

options.label: The severity rating is wrong
It names no specific code, no specific encounter, no clinical consequence, and no owner — there's nothing here a specific person could start doing tomorrow morning
It should have been filed as a Critical finding instead

feedback.severity: The severity might well be defensible on its own terms — the problem isn't the number attached to it, it's that nothing else in the finding gives anyone a concrete starting point regardless of what severity it's rated.
feedback.nothing_actionable: Right. "Several encounters" isn't a sample a coder can pull. "Lacking appropriate specificity" isn't a code an engineer can look up. "Improve coding specificity" isn't an action with an owner or a deadline. Every phrase in this finding is a category, not an instance — and a category can't be fixed, only an instance can.
feedback.critical: A higher severity rating wouldn't have made this any more actionable — it would just be a more urgently ignored finding, since the actual defect (nothing concrete to act on) is orthogonal to how severe it's rated.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This finding fails a specific, checkable test: **could a stranger, with no other context, start doing something in the next ten minutes because of this sentence?** "Several encounters" can't be pulled up. "Appropriate specificity" isn't defined anywhere the reader can check. "Improve coding specificity" has no owner and no definition of done. A usable version names one real encounter (or a short list), the exact code that was too broad and the one that should have been used, the clinical reason the gap matters, and who's expected to change what. The finding this module builds toward passes that ten-minute test every time.

contentSections.body: Notice what's missing isn't rigor — the underlying observation (codes lacking specificity in oncology) might be entirely correct. What's missing is the translation from a category of problem into an instance of it, concrete enough that someone can check it, reproduce it, and know when it's fixed. That translation is the actual skill this module teaches, and it's a writing skill sitting on top of the auditing skill from the last module — the audit finds the problem, the finding makes it fixable.

contentSections.question: If Finding 14 had kept the exact same severity rating and the exact same underlying observation, but named one specific patient encounter, the exact ICD-10-CM code used versus what the documentation actually supported, and the coder or team responsible for that encounter type — would it likely get fixed faster?
contentSections.answer: Yes, dramatically — nothing about the underlying facts changed, only the specificity of the writing. A reader can now verify the claim against a real record, understand exactly what's wrong, and know who's supposed to act. This is the whole lesson in miniature: actionability is almost entirely a writing property, not a rigor property.
contentSections.hint: Ask what changed between the two versions — was it the underlying truth, or just how concretely it was stated?

contentSections.body: A finding that names only categories — "several encounters," "appropriate specificity," "improve coding" — can be completely true and completely useless. Name the instance, not the category.

contentSections.title: What every finding needs, regardless of who reads it

contentSections.body: Before splitting a finding into what a clinician needs and what an engineer needs, there's a shared core both of them need identically — skipping it is what produced Finding 14.

contentSections.scenario: Consider what a rewritten Finding 14 needs before it can be split into clinician-facing and engineer-facing language.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in every finding, regardless of audience?

items.label: At least one specific, real (or realistically constructed) instance — an encounter, a code, a date
What the gap actually costs — a clinical consequence, stated in plain terms
Who is expected to act on it
Full technical terminology throughout, so nothing gets lost in translation
Enough detail that someone else could find the same instance independently

explanation.instance: Yes — this is the single fix that would have saved Finding 14. Without a real instance, there's nothing to verify and nothing to reproduce.
explanation.consequence: Yes — a reader has to know why this matters before they'll prioritize it, and "matters" has to be stated in terms of what happens to a patient or a decision, not just a rule that was broken.
explanation.owner: Yes — a finding with no named owner defaults to everyone's problem, which in practice means nobody's.
explanation.jargon: No — uniform jargon is exactly what makes a finding readable by only one of its two audiences. The shared core should avoid jargon that only one side understands; each audience's specific language comes later, layered on top of the shared core, not baked into it.
explanation.repro: Yes — if a reader can't independently arrive at the same instance you found, they can't verify the finding, and an unverifiable finding invites exactly the kind of dismissal this whole phase is trying to prevent.

contentSections.synthesis: Instance, consequence, owner, and reproducibility are the shared skeleton every finding needs before you write a single audience-specific word. The next four lessons build outward from this skeleton — toward a clinician and an engineer at once, toward reproduction steps, toward severity and urgency stated without crying wolf, toward a recommendation that actually names who does what.

contentSections.body: Every finding needs a real instance, a stated consequence, a named owner, and enough detail to reproduce — before you've written a single word aimed at either a clinician or an engineer specifically.

title: Clinical impact and technical cause in the same paragraph
description: A clinician who reads only the first sentence and an engineer who reads only the last one should both walk away knowing what to do — which means both have to live in the same paragraph, not separate sections.

learningObjectives.text: Write a finding whose first sentence carries clinical impact and whose supporting detail carries technical cause, in a single coherent paragraph

contentSections.title: Why splitting into two sections fails

contentSections.body: The instinctive fix for a two-audience problem is two sections: a "Clinical Summary" for the clinical lead and a "Technical Details" for engineering. It's a reasonable instinct and it's usually wrong, for a specific reason.

contentSections.scenario: A finding is written with a "Clinical Impact" section (two sentences, no code specifics) followed by a separate "Technical Root Cause" section (four sentences, no mention of patient impact). Both sections are individually well-written.
contentSections.question: What's the predictable failure mode of this two-section structure?

options.label: Nothing — each reader gets exactly the section they need

The engineer, reading only the technical section, never sees why the fix matters or how urgent it is; the clinician, reading only the clinical section, can't tell whether the proposed fix (once one exists) actually addresses the cause
The document becomes too long

feedback.fine: This is the appealing assumption, but in practice each reader stops at the section addressed to them — the engineer skims past "Clinical Impact" as not-my-job, and the clinical lead skims past "Technical Root Cause" as not-my-language. The two halves never actually connect for either reader.
feedback.disconnect: Right. Splitting into sections lets each reader's eyes slide past the half meant for someone else — which defeats the entire point of a two-audience finding. The engineer needs to feel the urgency to prioritize the fix correctly; the clinical lead needs enough of the mechanism to sanity-check whether a proposed fix actually addresses what's wrong, not just whether it sounds reassuring.
feedback.length: Length isn't really the issue — a well-integrated finding of similar total length works fine. The failure is structural, not about word count.

contentSections.concept: **A finding for two audiences has to put both audiences in the same sentence, not the same document.** The reliable pattern: open with the clinical consequence stated in a way anyone can understand, in the very next clause name the specific technical mechanism that causes it, and keep doing that — impact, mechanism, impact, mechanism — rather than front-loading one and appending the other.

contentSections.body: A worked comparison. Split version: *"Clinical Impact: Patients with a specific allergy history may not receive appropriate alerts. Technical Root Cause: The RxNorm mapping for X drug class defaults to a broader ingredient concept than the source documentation supports."* Integrated version: *"A patient allergic to codeine specifically — not opioids broadly — can be shown as allergic to the entire opioid class, because the coding tool's RxNorm mapping defaults drug-specific reactions up to the ingredient class whenever the source note doesn't explicitly state 'class-specific.' The result: a clinician sees a blanket opioid allergy and avoids an entire category of pain control the patient could safely use."* Same facts, but every clause carries both halves at once — nobody can read only part of it and miss the point.

Integrate impact and mechanism clause by clause, not section by section. A reader who only reads half the sentence should still get both halves — because in practice, that's exactly what happens with a split document.
This is a rewriting skill more than a composing-from-scratch skill — most of the raw material already exists in your audit notes from the last module. The work is weaving, not inventing.

contentSections.problem: You have two separate notes from your audit: (Clinical) "A stale 'penicillin allergy: severe' code blocks first-line antibiotic treatment for patients who could safely receive it." (Technical) "The allergy field has no re-verification step; severity defaults to 'severe' when abstracted from ambiguous source text." Combine them into one integrated finding.

steps.label: Start with the concrete instance and its clinical consequence
steps.work: "A patient's chart carries 'penicillin allergy: severe,' abstracted years earlier from a note that only described a mild childhood rash."
steps.why: Leading with a real instance and its human stakes earns the reader's attention before asking them to follow any mechanism — this is the same instance-first move from lesson 1, now doing double duty as the paragraph's opening.

steps.label: Immediately connect the mechanism, in the same breath
steps.work: "...because the allergy field's severity defaults to 'severe' whenever source text is ambiguous, and nothing re-verifies that default once it's set."
steps.why: The word "because" is doing the integration work — it forces mechanism and consequence into the same sentence instead of letting them live in separate paragraphs a reader might not connect.

steps.label: State the downstream effect concretely
steps.work: "As a result, this patient — and others coded the same way — is denied first-line penicillin treatment for infections where it would be the safest, most effective option."
steps.why: This closes the loop back to the clinical stakes, so the paragraph doesn't end on a purely technical note that a clinical reader might tune out of.

steps.label: Only then, add the specific technical detail an engineer needs to act
steps.work: "The default lives in the allergy-abstraction module's severity-assignment logic; there is no scheduled re-verification against updated source documentation."
steps.why: This sentence is allowed to be more technical, because it arrives after the reader — of either background — already understands why it matters. Technical specificity earned late reads as detail, not jargon.

faded.problem: Now integrate this pair yourself: (Clinical) "Patients with a stale 'active' depression diagnosis may not be re-screened, missing a genuine current episode." (Technical) "The depression-screening trigger checks only whether an active diagnosis code exists, with no check on when it was last confirmed."

blanks.prompt: What's the concrete opening move — instance plus consequence, in one clause?
blanks.answer: a patient with a stale active depression code is skipped for re-screening
accept: patient with stale active depression diagnosis isn't rescreened
stale depression code means no rescreening
blanks.why: Same move as the worked example: name the instance and what it costs before anything technical.

blanks.prompt: What word or phrase does the integrating work, connecting consequence to mechanism?
blanks.why: The connective word is what prevents the two halves from splitting back into separate sentences a reader could skim past independently.

blanks.prompt: What's the specific mechanism, stated so an engineer could locate it?
blanks.answer: the screening trigger checks only for an active diagnosis code, with no check on when it was last confirmed
accept: no re-confirmation check on the diagnosis code's recency
blanks.why: This is the exact, locatable defect — vague enough and it's back to Finding 14's problem; specific enough and an engineer knows where to look.

blanks.prompt: What's the downstream clinical effect, closing the loop?
blanks.answer: a genuinely at-risk patient's current depression episode goes undetected
blanks.why: Closing back on the human stakes is what keeps a clinical reader engaged through to the end of a technically-detailed finding.

contentSections.procedure: **Instance + consequence → connective ("because"/"since") → mechanism → downstream effect, closing the loop back to the patient.** Every finding in this module follows this shape, whether it's three sentences or ten.

contentSections.body: The integration procedure is mechanical once you see it: instance and consequence, a connective word, the mechanism, and a closing line back to the patient. Practice makes it fast, not just possible.

title: Reproduction steps for a clinical error
description: A finding someone can't reproduce is a finding they have to take on faith — and faith is exactly what an audit exists to replace with evidence.

learningObjectives.text: Write reproduction steps for a clinical coding error that another reviewer could follow independently

contentSections.title: What "reproducible" means for a coding error

contentSections.body: Reproduction steps for a software bug are a familiar idea: click here, see this, expect that. A coding error's reproduction steps look different, because there's usually no button to click — the defect is in what got recorded, not in an action someone takes.

contentSections.scenario: A finding states: "Reproduction: Open the patient's chart and review the allergy field. It will show an incorrect entry." A colleague tries to follow these steps on the named chart and can't tell what's supposedly wrong — the allergy field looks unremarkable to them.
contentSections.question: What's actually missing from these reproduction steps?

options.label: The chart identifier — they're looking at the wrong patient
A comparison point: what the source documentation actually says, so the colleague can see the mismatch, not just stare at an entry that looks fine on its own
A screenshot of the field

feedback.chart_id: The chart identifier is worth including, but even with the right chart, "it will show an incorrect entry" doesn't tell the colleague what *correct* would look like — they still can't tell whether what they're seeing is right or wrong without a comparison point.
feedback.comparison: Right. A coding error's reproduction isn't just "look here" — it's "look here, then look at the source, then notice they disagree." Without the source-document comparison, the colleague is being asked to spot a wrongness that only exists relative to something they haven't been shown.
feedback.screenshot: A screenshot (per the evidence standard from the last module) is genuinely useful backup, but it doesn't substitute for the actual reproduction *steps* — a colleague following steps should be able to independently arrive at the same conclusion, not just be shown your conclusion as a picture.

contentSections.mechanism: **A coding error's reproduction has three parts: where to look, what the source says, and what the coded field says instead** — the mismatch between the second and third is the entire finding, and steps that only point at the third part leave the reader unable to verify anything for themselves. This is the coding-specific version of a UI bug's "steps to reproduce": there's no click sequence, but there is a comparison sequence, and it needs to be just as explicit.

contentSections.body: A workable reproduction block for a coding finding has four lines: **Where** — chart/encounter identifier and the specific field. **Source** — the exact source text (or a close paraphrase with the original preserved as evidence per the last module) the code should have been derived from. **Coded as** — what the system actually shows. **Expected** — what the field should show, and why, in one clause. A reader who has never seen the chart can follow these four lines and arrive at your same conclusion, which is the entire test of whether a finding is reproducible.

contentSections.question: Why does "expected" need a one-clause reason attached, rather than just stating the expected code on its own?
contentSections.answer: Because stating only the expected value invites the reader to trust your judgment rather than check your reasoning — a one-clause reason ("...because the note describes a single-drug reaction, not a class-wide one") lets the reader verify the logic itself, not just take your conclusion on faith, which is the whole point of reproducibility.
contentSections.hint: Think about the difference between a reader trusting your conclusion versus a reader being able to check your reasoning.

contentSections.body: Reproduction steps for a coding error are: where to look, what the source actually says, what the code actually shows, and what it should show and why. A reader with no other context should reach your same conclusion by following those four lines.

The temptation to skip full reproduction steps is strongest exactly when you have the most findings and the least time — which is also when a skipped step costs the most, because nobody downstream has your context to fill the gap.

contentSections.title: Cutting corners under deadline pressure
contentSections.opening: You're finalizing a 14-finding report due in two hours. Finding 9 is clear in your head — you remember the chart, the mismatch, all of it — but writing the full four-line reproduction block for it will take another eight minutes you don't obviously have.

decide.situation: You could write "Reproduction: see chart notes, allergy field is miscoded" and move on, or take the eight minutes.
decide.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Write the shorthand version and move on — you'll remember the details if anyone asks
choices.consequence: Three weeks later, someone does ask, in a meeting you're not in. Nobody can answer, the finding gets marked "needs clarification," and it sits for another two weeks until you're available to explain it from memory.

choices.label: Take the eight minutes now, for this and every other finding you're tempted to shorthand
choices.consequence: The report takes slightly longer to finish, but every finding in it can be acted on by someone who has never talked to you.

choices.label: Write the shorthand version but flag it explicitly: "Reproduction steps abbreviated — full detail available from [you], request before acting"
choices.consequence: Better than silent shorthand — at least a reader knows not to trust it as self-contained — but it just relocates the eight minutes to a future interruption, at a worse time, with a colder trail.

delayed.summary: The finding sits, unusable, for weeks past when it could have been acted on, over eight minutes that felt expensive in the moment.
delayed.lesson: "You'll remember the details" is a bet against your own future memory and everyone else's availability, and it loses more often than it feels like it will while you're mid-deadline. The eight minutes are cheap now and expensive later, every time.

resolved.summary: Every finding in the report is independently actionable, including Finding 9, without anyone needing to track you down.
resolved.lesson: This is the actual cost-benefit of full reproduction steps: a fixed, small, predictable cost now, against an unpredictable and usually larger cost of someone needing you later and you being unavailable, on vacation, or having genuinely forgotten.

deferred.summary: The report is honest about its own gap, which is better than silently shipping an unreproducible finding — but the underlying work still has to happen eventually, at a less convenient time.
deferred.lesson: Flagging a shortcut honestly is real progress over hiding it, and worth doing when you genuinely can't do better. But it's a fallback, not a target — the goal is still full reproduction steps the first time, when you have the most context and the least reconstruction cost.

contentSections.body: Full reproduction steps cost a fixed, small amount of time when you write them, with the chart fresh in your head. Skipping them defers that cost to later, at a worse time, and often to someone who isn't you.

title: Severity, urgency, and not crying wolf
description: Rating everything Critical gets everything ignored just as surely as rating nothing Critical does — a report's credibility is a finite resource, spent one inflated severity at a time.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a written finding's stated severity and urgency actually match the facts as described

contentSections.body: The first report from a new audit team rates nine of twelve findings Critical. The second report from the same team, four months later, rates two of fifteen findings Critical — and gets far more of them fixed.

contentSections.scenario: In practice, once a reader has seen a handful of findings rated Critical that, on inspection, didn't reach the anchored-facts bar for Critical (reached the patient, harm not reversible), their trust in that team's severity ratings changes measurably.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many miscalibrated Critical ratings does it typically take before a reader starts mentally discounting every subsequent Critical rating from the same source, regardless of whether it's accurate?
contentSections.explanation: It doesn't take many — often just one or two visibly inflated ratings are enough for a reader to start applying a private discount to every future rating from that source, an effect that's well-documented in how people respond to any warning system that cries wolf. The asymmetry is brutal: inflating severity buys, at best, faster attention on this one finding; it costs calibrated trust on every finding after it, for as long as anyone remembers.

contentSections.body: The discipline is the same one from the last module: **rate by the anchored facts, not by how urgently you want it fixed.** A finding can be genuinely important — worth fixing soon, worth escalating — without meeting the anchored bar for Critical. The place for "this deserves priority even though it's technically Medium" is a separate urgency note, exactly as covered when the pharmacist near-miss came up earlier in this phase, not an inflated severity number. A report where every Critical really is Critical is a report whose next Critical gets read as urgent. A report where Critical has become the team's version of "please pay attention" has spent that word and can't get it back easily.
Severity inflation is a one-way trade: a little extra attention now, for a permanently discounted signal later. Rate by the facts; put genuine urgency in its own note.

contentSections.title: Stating urgency honestly, without underselling it

contentSections.body: The opposite failure is just as real: a genuinely urgent finding, written so cautiously that its urgency doesn't survive the translation onto the page.

contentSections.question: A finding about a genuinely dangerous, actively-occurring allergy-coding pattern (not hypothetical — it's producing wrong entries right now, in the current patient population) needs to convey real urgency without inflating its severity rating past what the facts support. Order these elements from most to least important for conveying that urgency honestly.
steps: State plainly that the pattern is active and ongoing, not historical — this is happening to current patients, right now
Give a concrete estimate of how many patients are likely currently affected, even if approximate
Name a specific, reasonable timeframe for a fix or mitigation, not an open-ended 'soon'
Use precise, non-inflated language throughout, letting the facts above carry the weight rather than intensifying adjectives
contentSections.explanation: Active-and-ongoing framing does the most work — a reader treats "this happened once, historically" very differently from "this is happening to people right now," independent of anything else in the finding. A concrete affected-count, even approximate, turns an abstract pattern into a scale a reader can weigh against other priorities. A specific timeframe converts "urgent" from a feeling into a request the reader can actually schedule against. And precise language throughout is what keeps all of the above credible — the moment intensifying adjectives creep in, a careful reader starts wondering whether the facts alone would have carried it.

contentSections.body: Real urgency is conveyed by facts — active and ongoing, an affected count, a specific timeframe — not by intensifying language. Precise words carrying real facts read as more urgent than dramatic words carrying vague ones.

title: Recommendations that name an owner
description: A recommendation with no named owner is a wish. The difference between a finding that gets fixed and one that gets filed is often nothing more than one clause naming who does what.

learningObjectives.text: Write a recommendation that names a specific owner, action, and a way to verify completion

contentSections.title: Recommendations that describe a wish, not a task

contentSections.body: "Improve coding specificity in oncology" from Finding 14 is a wish. So is "the mapping logic should be more careful" and "clinicians should double-check allergy fields." None of these has an owner, a concrete action, or a way to know when it's done.

contentSections.scenario: Compare two recommendations for the same underlying finding (a class-level allergy generalization defect): (A) "The allergy-mapping logic should not over-generalize drug-specific reactions." (B) "The engineering team owning the allergy-abstraction module should add a check requiring an explicit 'class-wide' flag before generalizing a single-drug reaction to a class-level allergy; target: next sprint. Verification: run the module against the 12 misclassified charts from this audit's sample and confirm all 12 resolve correctly."
contentSections.question: What makes (B) an actual recommendation rather than a restated wish?

options.label: It's longer and more detailed
It names who owns the change, what specifically changes, a rough timeframe, and a concrete way to verify it worked
It uses more technical language

feedback.length: Length isn't the operative difference — a recommendation could be four concise clauses and still hit all four elements. It's not about word count, it's about which four things those words actually say.
feedback.complete: Right. Owner (the engineering team owning that module), action (a specific check, described precisely enough to be built), timeframe (next sprint), and verification (re-run against the 12 known-bad charts) — all four are present and none of them require a follow-up meeting to clarify. (A) has none of the four; it just restates the problem in the imperative mood.
feedback.technical: More technical language on its own doesn't make something actionable — Finding 14's original version used perfectly correct technical terms ("specificity") and was still useless, because it had no owner, no concrete action, and no verification step.

contentSections.concept: **A recommendation is a task, not a description of the problem restated hopefully.** The four required parts — owner, specific action, timeframe, verification — turn a wish into something that can actually be assigned, tracked, and closed. Missing any one of the four degrades it back toward a wish: no owner means it's everyone's job (so nobody's); no specific action means the owner has to reverse-engineer what you actually want; no timeframe means it competes with nothing for priority; no verification means "done" is whoever says so.

contentSections.body: "Owner" deserves a specific note: it should almost never be an individual person by name — people change roles, go on leave, leave the organization — it should be a role or a team ("the engineering team owning the allergy-abstraction module," "the oncology coding lead"). A recommendation addressed to a person becomes stale the moment that person's job changes; one addressed to a role survives it.
A complete recommendation has an owner (a role, not a name), a specific action, a timeframe, and a way to verify it worked. Missing any one turns it back into a wish.

contentSections.title: When you don't control the fix

contentSections.body: Sometimes the honest owner of a fix is a vendor, or a team with competing priorities that will push back — and the recommendation still has to be written as a real task, not softened into something nobody's accountable for just because it's awkward to assign.

contentSections.question: A finding's fix genuinely requires a third-party coding-tool vendor to change their mapping logic — something you have zero direct control over. Does that mean the recommendation should stay vague ("vendor should be consulted") since you can't force the outcome?
contentSections.answer: No — the recommendation can still name a specific owner (whoever on your side owns the vendor relationship), a specific action (raise this exact defect, with this exact evidence, through the vendor's formal escalation channel, by a stated date), and a verification step (confirm the vendor's response and re-test). You can't control whether the vendor fixes it, but you can and should make the internal action fully owned and trackable — the next module covers working the vendor relationship itself in more depth.
contentSections.hint: Separate what you can't control (the vendor's fix) from what you can control (your own team's action to pursue it).

contentSections.body: Not controlling the fix doesn't excuse a vague recommendation. Name the owner and action for the part you do control — escalating, tracking, verifying — even when the actual fix belongs to someone else.

title: Practice — Rewrite Eight Unusable Findings
description: Eight findings in the Finding-14 style — accurate, unusable. Rewrite each so a stranger could act on it in under ten minutes.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the instance/consequence/mechanism/owner structure to rewrite unusable findings across varied scenarios

contentSections.body: Same drill format as the last two modules — no new ideas, just reps turning vague, accurate findings into ones a stranger could act on.
Every rewrite in this set follows the same shape: real instance, integrated impact and mechanism, honest severity, owned recommendation.

title: Lab — Write the Report for Your Audit
description: Take the audit you ran in the last module's lab (or a fresh scenario) and produce a full report: executive summary, integrated findings, honest severities, and owned recommendations.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a complete audit report with an executive summary, integrated findings, calibrated severities, and owned recommendations

contentSections.body: If you completed the previous module's audit lab, use its findings as raw material — this lab is about turning what you found into something that gets acted on. If you're starting fresh, the brief below gives you enough to work with.

contentSections.title: Write the Report for Your Audit
contentSections.brief: Write a complete audit report covering at least 5 findings — reuse your findings from the previous lab if you have them, or construct 5 realistic findings from the oncology/ED scenario used there. The report needs an executive summary a director will actually read, and each finding written so a clinician and an engineer could both act on it without a follow-up meeting.
contentSections.deliverable: A report document: a one-paragraph executive summary (top risks, in plain language, no jargon); 5+ findings, each following the instance/consequence/mechanism/owner structure from this module, with honest severity ratings and full reproduction steps; a recommendations table naming an owner, action, timeframe, and verification step for each finding.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Draft each finding's core
stages.instructions: For each finding, write the integrated instance + consequence + mechanism paragraph from lesson 2's procedure. Don't add severity or recommendations yet.
stages.checkpoint: You have 5+ integrated finding paragraphs, each passing the ten-minute actionability test from lesson 1.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Add reproduction steps and rate severity
stages.instructions: Add the four-line reproduction block (where, source, coded as, expected) to each finding. Then rate each one's severity using the anchored facts, separately from writing — per the staging discipline from the previous module.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has reproduction steps and a fact-justified severity rating.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Write recommendations
stages.instructions: For each finding, write a recommendation with a named owner (role, not person), specific action, timeframe, and verification step, per lesson 5.
stages.checkpoint: Every recommendation has all four required parts.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Write the executive summary and assemble
stages.instructions: Write a one-paragraph executive summary naming the top 2-3 risks in plain language, then assemble the full report: summary, findings, recommendations table, in that order.
stages.checkpoint: You have one document, start to finish, that a director could read the summary of in 30 seconds and an engineer could act on a finding from without asking a follow-up question.

rubric.criterion: Findings are integrated, not split by audience
rubric.meets: Clinical impact and technical mechanism appear woven together within each finding, not in separate sections.

rubric.criterion: Reproduction steps are complete
rubric.meets: Every finding has where/source/coded-as/expected, specific enough for an independent reader to reach the same conclusion.

rubric.criterion: Severity is calibrated, not inflated or undersold
rubric.meets: Every severity rating is justified by the anchored facts; urgency beyond the severity rating, if any, is stated as a separate note.

rubric.criterion: Recommendations are complete tasks
rubric.meets: Every recommendation names an owner (role), a specific action, a timeframe, and a verification step.

rubric.criterion: Executive summary is genuinely readable in 30 seconds
rubric.meets: A non-technical reader gets the top risks in plain language, with no jargon requiring the rest of the report to decode.

contentSections.body: This report is the actual product of a patient-safety audit — everything from scoping through evidence in the last module exists to produce findings that read like this one.

title: Checkpoint — Writing Findings Two Audiences Can Act On
description: Ungraded retrieval — third module of the phase, first with a real spaced pull: 4 from this module, 4 from How Coding Errors Reach Patients / Running a Safety Audit, 2 reaching back across both.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's writing standards alongside the chain and audit frameworks from earlier in the phase

contentSections.title: What stuck, and what's still there from before
Checkpoint — Writing Findings Two Audiences Can Act On
contentSections.framing: Ten questions: four from this module, four pulling back to the last two modules, and two reaching across everything so far in the phase.

questions.prompt: What test does a finding like "several encounters show specificity issues, improve coding specificity" fail?

options.label: Whether a stranger could start acting on it within about ten minutes
Whether it's grammatically correct
Whether it cites a specific ICD-10-CM code

questions.explanation: The actionability test is whether a reader with no other context could do something concrete because of the sentence — category-level language like "several encounters" and "improve specificity" fails that test regardless of grammar or citation.

questions.prompt: Why does splitting a finding into separate "Clinical Impact" and "Technical Root Cause" sections tend to fail?

options.label: Each reader's eyes tend to slide past the section not addressed to them, so the two halves never connect for anyone
It's against formatting standards
It makes the document too short

questions.explanation: Readers self-select into the section meant for them and skip the rest, defeating the purpose of a two-audience finding — integration at the clause level keeps both audiences engaged with the whole thing.

questions.prompt: What are the four lines a coding-error reproduction block needs?

options.label: Where to look, what the source says, what the code shows, and what it should show and why
Severity, urgency, owner, and timeframe
A screenshot, a date, a reviewer name, and a case number

questions.explanation: A coding error's reproduction is a comparison sequence — where, source, coded-as, expected-and-why — that lets a reader independently verify the mismatch, distinct from the severity/urgency/owner elements of a recommendation.

questions.prompt: What are the four required parts of a complete recommendation?

options.label: A named owner (role), a specific action, a timeframe, and a verification step
A severity rating, a due date, a signature, and an evidence file
A summary, a citation, a chart ID, and a reviewer name

questions.explanation: Missing owner, action, timeframe, or verification each degrade a recommendation back toward an unassignable wish — those four parts are what make it a trackable task.

questions.prompt: What three anchoring facts does a workable severity scale use instead of adjectives?

options.label: Whether it reached the patient, whether the harm was reversible, and how many steps it was caught from harm
How senior the clinician was, how old the record is, and how embarrassing the finding is
The exact code involved, its billing weight, and its character length

questions.explanation: Reached-patient, reversibility, and steps-from-harm are the concrete, checkable facts that let independent reviewers land on the same severity category.

questions.prompt: Why does pure random sampling tend to miss dangerous error clusters in low-volume, high-risk units?

options.label: Random sampling draws charts proportional to volume, structurally underrepresenting rare, severe clusters in low-volume areas
Random sampling always deliberately excludes small units
It doesn't — random sampling reliably catches every cluster given enough time

questions.explanation: A low-volume unit gets proportionally few random draws regardless of how dangerous its errors are per chart — exactly the gap risk-stratified sampling is built to close.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether something counts as durable audit evidence rather than narrative?

options.label: Whether it would still prove the finding if the system changed and everyone's memory of the details faded
Whether it was written by a senior reviewer
Whether it's longer than three sentences

questions.explanation: A screenshot or verbatim source text survives independent of memory or system changes; a paraphrase, however accurate it feels, does not.

questions.prompt: In the five-link chain framework, what's the difference between the origin link and a recovery link?

options.label: The origin is where the wrong fact was created; a recovery link is any later point that could have caught it
They're the same thing described two ways
The origin is always the clinician

questions.explanation: The origin is a single point of creation; recovery links are every subsequent checkpoint with a chance, missed or taken, to catch the error before it reached the patient.

questions.prompt: Connecting this module back to module 1's chain framework: why does a well-written finding's reproduction block matter for the same reason the chain's origin link matters?

options.label: Both are about locating the actual point of defect precisely, rather than describing the problem at the vague level where it was first noticed
They're unrelated — the chain framework is about causes, findings are about writing style
Reproduction steps only matter for near-misses, and the chain framework only matters for harm events

questions.explanation: Both skills fight the same failure mode: staying at the vague, first-noticed level of a problem ("a coding error contributed to harm" / "specificity issues in oncology") instead of locating the precise instance and mechanism — one for diagnosing where a chain broke, the other for writing it up so someone else can verify and fix it.

questions.prompt: Connecting this module back to module 2's severity work: why does calibrated (non-inflated) severity in a written finding depend on the anchored-facts scale specifically, rather than on the writer's judgment about urgency?

options.label: Because a reader's trust in a source's severity ratings degrades quickly once even one or two ratings turn out to be inflated relative to the facts — the anchored scale is what keeps ratings comparable and credible across an entire report
It doesn't depend on the scale — urgency and severity are the same thing and should always match
Only the most senior reviewer's judgment should determine severity, regardless of the scale

questions.explanation: This module's severity-inflation lesson is a direct application of module 2's anchored scale: rating by fact rather than by how badly you want something fixed is what preserves a report's credibility finding after finding.

contentSections.body: Writing a finding well is downstream of everything in this phase so far — the chain framework tells you what to look for, the audit method tells you how to find it rigorously, and this module turns what you found into something that actually gets fixed.

title: Why correct findings don't get fixed
description: A finding can be true, well-written, correctly owned, and still die in a backlog — because being right was never the bottleneck.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the non-technical reasons a correct, well-written finding fails to get fixed

contentSections.body: A perfectly written finding — real instance, integrated impact and mechanism, honest severity, full reproduction, an owned recommendation with a timeframe — sits open for eight months. Nothing about the writing was the problem. Everything else was.

contentSections.scenario: The eight-month-old finding is about a class-level allergy overgeneralization defect, correctly scoped and rated Medium. The engineering team it's assigned to has 40 open tickets, all technically valid, competing for the same two developers' time.
contentSections.question: What's the actual obstacle here?

options.label: The finding is somehow still not specific enough
A correctly-owned, correctly-rated finding is competing against 39 other correctly-owned findings for the same scarce capacity, and nothing in the finding itself resolves that competition
The severity rating was set too low to matter

feedback.specificity: This finding already passes every standard from the last module — real instance, integrated writing, honest severity, full reproduction, owned recommendation. Specificity was never the gap here; the writing quality of a finding has essentially nothing to do with whether it wins a prioritization fight against 39 others.
feedback.competition: Right. A well-written finding earns the *right* to be prioritized fairly — it doesn't win the prioritization fight by itself. Forty valid, competing demands on two people's time is a capacity and prioritization problem, and no amount of additional writing quality on any single finding solves a capacity problem.
feedback.severity: Raising the severity rating on a genuinely Medium finding to force it up the queue reintroduces exactly the inflation problem from the last module — it doesn't fix the underlying capacity constraint, it just breaks the scale's calibration for the next finding too.

contentSections.concept: **A finding can be perfect and still lose a prioritization fight it was never designed to win.** The skills in the last module get a finding taken seriously on its own merits. This module is about the separate skill of getting it actually scheduled against everything else competing for the same limited capacity — which requires understanding *why* things don't get fixed, not just writing them better.

contentSections.body:
Findings die for a small number of recurring reasons that have nothing to do with whether they were true or well-written:

- **Capacity competition** — correct findings queued behind other correct findings, with no mechanism forcing a choice between them.
- **No forcing function** — nothing ever makes *not* fixing it cost anything, so it's always rational to defer one more sprint.
- **Ambiguous ownership at the team level**, even when a role was correctly named — "the coding-tool team" might span three sub-teams who each assume another owns it.
- **The fix requires a decision nobody has authority to make alone** — a policy tradeoff, a vendor contract change, a cross-team resourcing call.

Diagnosing which of these is actually blocking a specific stuck finding is the first move — different blockers need different interventions, and treating a capacity problem as if it were an ownership problem (or vice versa) wastes the exact limited capacity you're trying to protect.

contentSections.question: If the eight-month-stuck finding's real blocker is capacity competition against 39 other valid tickets, what's the most useful next move — writing an even more detailed version of the finding, or something else entirely?
contentSections.answer: Something else — likely raising the prioritization decision itself to whoever has authority over that team's roadmap, with the finding's evidence as backup, rather than adding more detail to a document that was never the bottleneck. More writing on an already-complete finding doesn't create capacity or force a prioritization decision.
contentSections.hint: Ask what resource is actually scarce here — clarity about the problem, or time to work on it.

contentSections.body: A stuck finding usually isn't stuck because it was written badly. It's stuck because of capacity competition, a missing forcing function, diffuse ownership, or a decision above the finding's own authority level — diagnose which, before doing anything else.

contentSections.title: The difference between fixing an instance and fixing the pipeline

contentSections.body: A finding gets "fixed" — the one chart it named gets corrected. Six weeks later, the exact same defect produces a new wrong code in a different chart. Something got fixed. It wasn't the thing that mattered.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer finds a class-level allergy overgeneralization on a specific patient's chart, files a finding, and a coder manually corrects that one chart. The finding gets marked resolved. Two months later, an identical pattern — same underlying mapping defect — appears on three new patients.
contentSections.question: What actually went wrong with how this finding was closed?

options.label: The coder who fixed the chart made a mistake
The instance was corrected but the pipeline defect that produced it was never touched, so the same defect kept generating the same error for every new patient it applied to
The finding should never have been marked resolved without a second reviewer

feedback.coder: The coder did exactly what they were asked — correct this one chart. Nothing about their individual action was wrong; the gap is in what "resolved" was allowed to mean.
feedback.instance_vs_pipeline: Right. Correcting one chart is patient-level remediation — necessary, but it doesn't touch the mapping logic that produced the error in the first place. "Resolved" got applied to the instance when the actual defect, the thing this whole phase's chain framework points at as the origin, was never addressed.
feedback.second_reviewer: A second reviewer might have caught that the underlying defect was untouched, but that's a review-process fix layered on top of the real gap — the actual problem is that "resolved" was defined at the wrong level in the first place, for anyone reviewing it.

contentSections.mechanism: **Every finding closure should distinguish two separate questions: was this instance corrected, and was the pipeline that produced it changed?** "Resolved" should never mean only the first one for a finding whose whole point was identifying a systemic defect — this is the same distinction from this phase's very first module, applied now to remediation instead of diagnosis: fixing the chart closest to you is not the same as fixing the origin.

contentSections.body: "Resolved" has to answer two questions, not one: was this specific instance corrected, and was the pipeline defect that produced it actually changed. A finding closed on the first alone will keep reproducing itself.

title: Fixing the pipeline versus fixing the review step
description: When a defect keeps recurring, there are usually two different places you could intervene — upstream in the pipeline that creates the error, or downstream in the review step that's supposed to catch it. They're not equally good choices.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a proposed fix targets the pipeline or the review step, and what each choice trades off

contentSections.title: Two places to intervene, not equally good

contentSections.body: For almost any recurring defect, there's a version of the fix that changes the thing producing the error, and a version that adds a check to catch it afterward. Both count as "fixing" the finding. They are not equally durable.

contentSections.scenario: A recurring drug-mapping error (look-alike names defeating a string match, similar to the metoprolol/metolazone pattern from earlier in this phase) has two candidate fixes on the table: (A) require pharmacist sign-off on any mapping below a confidence threshold; (B) replace the string-similarity matching with a verified code-table lookup that doesn't rely on string distance at all.
contentSections.question: Evaluate each fix on durability and cost — which properties apply to which?

items.label: (A) catches errors after they're generated, adding review burden indefinitely
(B) prevents the error class from being generated at all, at a one-time engineering cost
(A) is typically cheaper and faster to implement right now
(B) has no ongoing human-review cost once built, unlike (A)
(A) permanently eliminates the underlying string-matching defect

explanation.a_catches: True — a review-step fix like pharmacist sign-off doesn't touch the mapping logic; it adds a human check downstream of a defect that keeps producing candidates for that human to catch, forever.
explanation.b_prevents: True — replacing the matching method addresses the actual generative mechanism, so the specific error class (look-alike string collisions) stops being possible, not just stops slipping through unnoticed.
explanation.a_cheap_now: True, and this is the real, honest tradeoff — a review-step fix is almost always faster and cheaper to ship this sprint, which is exactly why it's tempting even when it's the less durable choice.
explanation.b_no_ongoing: True — once built, a verified lookup carries no per-case human review cost, unlike a sign-off requirement that costs a little bit of pharmacist time on every single low-confidence mapping, forever.
explanation.a_permanent: False — this is the trap. A review step doesn't eliminate anything; it manages the consequences of a defect that's still fully present and will still generate wrong candidates indefinitely, relying on the review step never lapsing.

contentSections.synthesis: **Neither option is wrong on its own — the mistake is treating a review-step fix as equivalent to a pipeline fix when reporting the finding as resolved.** A review-step fix is a legitimate, often necessary *interim* mitigation, especially when the pipeline fix will take months. The failure mode is stopping there permanently because the interim fix made the symptom go away.

contentSections.body: A useful frame: a review-step fix trades an ongoing cost (review time, review fatigue, the risk that the review step itself gets skipped under pressure — echoing the alert-fatigue mechanism from earlier in this phase) for a lower upfront cost. A pipeline fix trades a higher upfront cost for eliminating the ongoing one. Both are sometimes the right call — a pipeline fix six months out is not a reason to leave patients exposed today, so a review-step interim measure is often exactly right *as an interim measure, explicitly labeled as one*, with the pipeline fix still tracked as the actual resolution.

A review-step fix manages a defect's consequences; a pipeline fix eliminates the defect. Use the review-step fix as an explicit interim measure when needed — but don't let it quietly become the permanent answer.

contentSections.title: When the review step actually is the right permanent answer

contentSections.body: This isn't a universal rule that pipeline fixes always win. Sometimes a review step is the correct permanent design, and knowing which case you're in matters as much as knowing the general preference.

contentSections.scenario: Consider a case where automating the pipeline fix would require the AI-assisted coding tool to make a judgment call the source documentation genuinely doesn't resolve — for example, distinguishing a documented side effect from a true allergy when a note is itself ambiguous about which it is.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of coding ambiguities that reach a human reviewer are, on inspection, cases where the source documentation itself is genuinely ambiguous — not cases where a smarter pipeline could have resolved it automatically?
contentSections.explanation: It's a meaningful minority, not the majority and not negligible — a real share of ambiguous cases trace back to source documentation that itself doesn't specify enough to resolve automatically, no matter how good the mapping logic gets. For that share, a human review step isn't an interim workaround for a pipeline gap; it's the actually-correct permanent design, because the judgment call requires information a pipeline cannot manufacture. The skill is telling these apart from the much larger share of cases (like the look-alike-name mapping defect) where a pipeline fix genuinely could resolve the ambiguity, and a review step is only ever a stopgap for those.

contentSections.body: When the ambiguity lives in the source documentation itself, not in the pipeline's matching logic, a human review step is the correct permanent design — not a stopgap. Tell the two cases apart before recommending a fix.

title: Feeding corrections back so the same error stops recurring
description: A one-off correction that never reaches the system that generated the error is a promise that the same error will happen again, to someone else.

learningObjectives.text: Design a feedback loop that routes a correction back into whatever generated the original error

contentSections.body: A coder catches and fixes a mismapped drug name in a chart. The correction lives in that chart. The AI-assisted coding tool that produced the wrong mapping in the first place has no idea a mistake happened, and will produce the identical wrong mapping for the next patient whose discharge note uses the same phrasing.

contentSections.code:
Correction workflow (as currently implemented):

  1. Coder identifies mismapped drug in chart review
  2. Coder manually corrects the chart's medication list
  3. Chart is marked reviewed and complete

(No step routes the correction anywhere else.)
contentSections.question: What's structurally missing from this workflow?

options.label: A step where the coder documents why the mapping was wrong
Any mechanism that feeds the correction back to the mapping tool or its training/reference data, so the same wrong mapping doesn't get generated again
A supervisor sign-off before marking the chart complete

feedback.documents: Documenting the reasoning is good practice for the chart-level record, but it doesn't change what happens the next time the same source phrasing hits the same mapping tool — the documentation lives in a chart nobody reviewing the mapping logic will ever read.
feedback.feedback_loop: Right. This workflow is a closed loop at the chart level and an open, leaking one at the system level — nothing captures the individual correction and routes it toward the actual defect. The next patient with the same discharge phrasing gets the exact same wrong mapping.
feedback.signoff: A sign-off step adds a second set of eyes on this one chart, but it's a review-step addition, not a feedback mechanism — it doesn't get the correction anywhere near the mapping tool that generated the original error.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A correction workflow with no feedback loop treats every instance of the same underlying defect as a brand-new, unrelated problem, discovered and manually fixed from scratch each time — which is both wasteful of reviewer effort and, more importantly, means every instance between the first discovery and the eventual pipeline fix reaches a new patient with zero benefit from the last correction. The fix is structural: every correction needs a second destination beyond the chart it happened on — a defect log, a training-data correction queue, a vendor escalation ticket — something that accumulates evidence toward the actual pipeline fix.

contentSections.body: A workable feedback loop has three properties: **it's automatic or near-automatic** (not an extra optional step a busy coder will skip under pressure); **it accumulates**, so five instances of the same defect visibly become one pattern rather than five isolated corrections nobody connects; and **it's visible to whoever owns the pipeline fix**, not buried in a chart-level audit trail only reviewers ever look at. The correction itself was never the hard part — coders correct mismapped drugs constantly. The hard part is making that correction count toward something bigger than the one chart it happened on.

contentSections.question: If five different coders independently correct the same underlying mapping defect on five different charts over two months, but none of those corrections are logged anywhere connecting them, what happens to the audit's ability to make the case for a pipeline fix?
contentSections.answer: It's severely weakened — the case for prioritizing a pipeline fix over other competing work is much stronger as "this exact defect has recurred five times in two months, here's the pattern" than as five separate, disconnected chart corrections nobody has assembled into a pattern. Without the feedback loop, the strongest evidence for prioritization never gets built.
contentSections.hint: Think back to lesson 1's point about correct findings competing for scarce capacity — what makes one finding win that competition?

contentSections.body: A correction with no feedback loop is wasted twice: once because the same error will recur, and again because the recurrence pattern that would justify prioritizing a pipeline fix never gets assembled.

contentSections.title: Building the loop without slowing everyone down

contentSections.body: The objection to any feedback-loop proposal is predictable: "we don't have time to add a step to every correction." The objection is often right about a badly-designed loop and wrong about a well-designed one.

contentSections.intro: Design a lightweight correction-feedback mechanism for the medication-mapping scenario, minimizing added burden on the coder making the correction.

fields.prompt: How should the correction get captured, given coders are already busy?
options: Reuse the existing correction action itself as the capture trigger — logging happens automatically when the chart field is edited, with no extra step for the coder
Require the coder to separately fill out a defect report form
Rely on coders to remember to email the engineering team
fields.correctValue: Reuse the existing correction action itself as the capture trigger — logging happens automatically when the chart field is edited, with no extra step for the coder
fields.feedback: Automating capture from an action the coder was already taking removes the "extra step" objection entirely — there's nothing new to remember or skip.

fields.prompt: How should individual corrections become a visible pattern?
options: Group logged corrections by defect signature (e.g. same source-phrase-to-wrong-mapping pattern) so a count accumulates automatically, visible without anyone manually connecting the dots
Leave them as a flat list for someone to review manually if they think to
Don't bother — the engineering team will notice a pattern eventually
fields.correctValue: Group logged corrections by defect signature (e.g. same source-phrase-to-wrong-mapping pattern) so a count accumulates automatically, visible without anyone manually connecting the dots
fields.feedback: Automatic grouping is what turns five isolated events into one visible, three-instances-and-counting pattern — exactly the evidence that wins a prioritization argument.

fields.prompt: Who should see the accumulated pattern, and how?
options: The team that owns the pipeline/mapping logic, via a dashboard or recurring report — not buried in a chart-level audit log only reviewers open
Only the original coder who made each correction
Nobody until the next formal audit cycle
fields.correctValue: The team that owns the pipeline/mapping logic, via a dashboard or recurring report — not buried in a chart-level audit log only reviewers open
fields.feedback: Visibility has to reach the people with authority to act on the pattern — a perfectly accumulated pattern nobody with fix authority ever sees is functionally the same as no feedback loop at all.

contentSections.synthesis: A good feedback loop rides on top of work coders are already doing, accumulates automatically into a pattern, and surfaces that pattern to whoever can act on it — it should cost the coder nothing extra and cost the pipeline owner nothing to interpret.

contentSections.body: The objection that a feedback loop slows people down is a design flaw, not an inherent tradeoff — a loop that piggybacks on an action already being taken adds no extra step and still produces the accumulated evidence a pipeline fix needs.

title: Working with the vendor whose product is wrong
description: When the defect lives in a third-party product, the skills shift from engineering influence to relationship and evidence management — and the stakes for getting that right don't go down.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate what a health system can and can't control when a patient-safety defect lives in a vendor's product

contentSections.body: A defect lives in the AI-assisted coding vendor's proprietary mapping model. You cannot see its training data, cannot modify its logic, and cannot deploy a fix yourself. This sounds like it removes your leverage entirely. It removes some of it, not all.

contentSections.scenario: You've documented a recurring, safety-relevant mapping defect (three instances, per the feedback-loop pattern from the last lesson) in a vendor's coding tool. The vendor's standard support channel has a three-week response SLA and no severity-based escalation path visible to you.
contentSections.question: What's actually within your control here, given you can't fix the vendor's code?

options.label: Nothing meaningful — you're entirely dependent on the vendor's own priorities

How rigorously you document and escalate the pattern, what contractual or regulatory levers exist (safety-relevant defects often have faster paths than standard support), and whether an interim mitigation protects patients while you wait
Whether to simply stop using the vendor's product immediately

feedback.nothing: This undersells your actual leverage. You don't control the vendor's engineering priorities, but you control the quality and forcefulness of the case you make, which channel you make it through, and what protects patients in the meantime — all of which meaningfully affect the outcome even without direct code access.
feedback.controllable: Right. This mirrors the recommendation-writing lesson from the last module, scaled up: you can't force the fix, but you can fully own your side — building an evidence package strong enough to justify escalation past the standard support queue, using contractual safety-defect clauses or regulatory reporting obligations where they exist (covered further in the governance module), and putting an interim mitigation in place so patients aren't exposed while the vendor timeline plays out.
feedback.stop_using: Switching vendors is sometimes eventually the right call, but it's rarely available as an immediate response to one defect — replacing a coding tool is a major undertaking with its own risks, and treating it as the default first move skips past every lower-cost lever that might actually work faster.

contentSections.concept: **Vendor dependency changes what you can do, not whether you can do anything.** The same discipline from writing an ownable recommendation when you don't control the fix — name what your side does, even when the actual fix is someone else's — scales up to the vendor relationship: escalation, evidence, and interim mitigation are all within your control even when the code isn't.

contentSections.body: Three levers worth knowing about specifically: **contractual safety-defect clauses** — many vendor agreements for clinical software include faster response commitments for patient-safety-relevant defects specifically, separate from general support SLAs, and it's worth knowing whether yours does before you need it. **Regulatory reporting** — depending on how the tool is classified, a safety-relevant defect may trigger an obligation to report to the vendor and, in some cases, a regulator, which is covered in more depth in the governance module but is worth flagging here as a genuine escalation lever, not just a compliance chore. **Interim mitigation on your side** — you don't need the vendor's fix to add a review-step check (per lesson 2) on your own end while you wait, even if it's not the permanent answer.
Not controlling the vendor's code doesn't mean not controlling the outcome. Escalation quality, contractual and regulatory levers, and interim mitigation are all real levers that stay in your hands.

contentSections.title: Building the evidence package that actually moves a vendor

contentSections.body: "Your product has a bug" gets a three-week queue position. A specific, evidenced, safety-framed escalation gets a different conversation.

contentSections.question: Order these elements of a vendor escalation package by how much weight they typically carry in moving a vendor past a standard support queue, most persuasive first.
steps: A pattern of multiple independent occurrences, not a single anecdote — the accumulated feedback-loop evidence from the last lesson
Explicit framing of the patient-safety consequence, not just a technical description of the defect
