Full reproduction steps the vendor's own engineers can follow without needing your health system's specific chart access
A reference to the specific contractual or regulatory obligation that applies, if one does
contentSections.explanation: A pattern beats an anecdote because vendors, like your own engineering team, triage by frequency and impact — one occurrence looks like noise, three or five look like a defect. Explicit safety framing changes which internal team at the vendor even sees the ticket; "data quality issue" and "patient safety defect" often route to entirely different response paths. Reproduction steps the vendor can act on without your systems remove the single biggest excuse for delay — needing to first spend a support cycle just understanding what you're describing. And contractual or regulatory references, while genuinely powerful, work best as backup to an already-strong technical and safety case, not as a substitute for one.

contentSections.body: A vendor escalation moves fastest with a documented pattern, explicit safety framing, vendor-actionable reproduction steps, and contractual or regulatory backup where it exists — in roughly that order of weight.

title: Verifying a fix actually fixed it
description: A fix that's shipped is not the same as a fix that worked — and the gap between those two states is exactly where the same defect quietly comes back.

learningObjectives.text: Design a verification check that confirms a deployed fix actually resolved the original defect, not just that something changed

contentSections.body: An engineering team reports the mapping logic fix is live. Everyone treats the finding as closed. Nobody actually re-ran the twelve known-bad charts from the original audit sample against the new logic to confirm they now map correctly.

contentSections.scenario: The vendor confirms a patch is deployed addressing the escalated mapping defect. Three months later, during an unrelated routine sample, a reviewer finds a new instance of the exact same mapping error — the same source phrasing producing the same wrong drug.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation, given the vendor confirmed deployment?

options.label: The vendor lied about deploying anything
The patch was deployed but never verified against the specific known-bad cases, so a partial fix, a regression, or a narrower-than-needed fix went undetected
This is simply an unrelated, brand-new defect that happens to look identical

feedback.lied: Vendors rarely fabricate deployment claims outright — the far more common failure is a real deployment that doesn't fully or correctly address the specific defect it was meant to, which is exactly why verification against the actual known-bad cases matters more than a deployment confirmation.
feedback.unverified: Right. A patch being deployed tells you something changed. It doesn't tell you the specific defect you reported is actually gone — the fix could be narrower than the real problem, could have an edge case the vendor's own testing missed, or could have been correct at deploy time and regressed in a later unrelated update. Only re-testing the known-bad cases closes that gap.
feedback.coincidence: Treating an identical failure pattern as an unrelated coincidence is exactly the assumption that lets a genuinely unresolved defect hide behind a deployment confirmation — the far more likely explanation, given identical source phrasing and identical wrong output, is that the original defect was never fully fixed.

contentSections.mechanism: **A deployment confirmation is a claim, not evidence — and this phase has spent two modules establishing that claims need evidence.** The same discipline applies to closing a finding as to opening one: don't mark it resolved on a vendor's or a colleague's say-so alone. Re-run the exact charts, cases, or scenarios from the original finding against the new system and confirm, directly, that they now produce the correct result.

contentSections.body: A minimal verification check, directly reusing the original finding's evidence: take the specific instance(s) captured when the finding was written (per this phase's evidence standard), re-run them — or realistic equivalents, if the originals can no longer be replayed — against the fixed system, and confirm the expected output now matches. This is cheap precisely because the evidence was already captured; it's only expensive if the original finding skipped preserving reproducible evidence, which is one more reason that discipline from earlier in this phase pays off here, potentially months later.

Don't close a finding on a deployment confirmation alone. Re-run the original known-bad cases against the fixed system and confirm the expected output — verification is cheap when the original evidence was captured properly, and it's the only thing that actually closes the loop.

contentSections.title: Watching for regression, not just confirming the fix once

contentSections.body: A fix verified once, on the day it shipped, can still silently break later — a subsequent unrelated update, a data migration, a model retrain can all reintroduce a defect that was genuinely fixed at one point.

contentSections.title: The fix that came back
contentSections.opening: Six months after a verified mapping-logic fix, a routine audit sample turns up the exact same defect pattern again. Checking the vendor's release notes, an unrelated model update three months ago appears to have reset some mapping behavior.

response.situation: The original finding was closed as resolved and verified at the time. It's now clearly back.
response.question: What's the right response?

choices.label: Reopen the original finding and re-escalate it as if starting fresh
choices.consequence: The vendor treats it as a new report and it re-enters the standard queue, losing the context and urgency that the original pattern-plus-verification history should carry.

choices.label: Reopen it explicitly flagged as a regression of a previously-verified fix, attaching the original evidence, the verification record, and the new instance
choices.consequence: The vendor's own process treats regressions of confirmed fixes differently from fresh reports — this routes faster and also raises a legitimate question about what in their release process let a verified fix silently regress.

choices.label: Assume verification once is sufficient going forward and don't build in any recurring check
choices.consequence: This is the same trap in a new form — a one-time verification was necessary but not, on its own, sufficient for a system that keeps changing underneath the fix.

reset.summary: The defect does eventually get re-fixed, but slower than it needed to, and the pattern of a fix regressing goes unexamined.
reset.lesson: Losing the history of a regression treats a systemic reliability question — why did a verified fix come back? — as if it never happened, wasting the strongest evidence you had.

resolved.summary: The vendor fixes it faster and, notably, also investigates why their release process allowed a regression, which the original bare finding never would have prompted.
resolved.lesson: Explicitly labeling a regression as a regression does two things a fresh report doesn't: it carries forward the urgency evidence already built, and it asks a second, more important question about the vendor's own process reliability.

recurs.summary: Without any periodic re-check built in, the same defect returns a third time before anyone notices, on a normal audit cycle rather than because anything flagged it.
recurs.lesson: A fix verified once against a system that continues to change is a snapshot, not a guarantee. High-risk, previously-defective areas deserve a standing check on future audit samples, not a closed case treated as permanently settled.

contentSections.body: A verified fix in a system that keeps changing is a snapshot, not a guarantee. Flag regressions as regressions, not fresh reports, and build previously-defective areas into future audit samples rather than treating them as permanently closed.

title: Practice — Choose the Intervention Point for Eight Recurring Errors
description: Eight recurring-defect scenarios: for each, choose between a review-step fix and a pipeline fix, design a feedback loop, or evaluate a vendor escalation — no new concepts, just judgment under varied constraints.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the pipeline-versus-review-step, feedback-loop, and verification frameworks to novel recurring-error scenarios

contentSections.body: Same drill format as the rest of this phase — reps, not new ideas. Each scenario asks you to choose where to intervene and why, using this module's frameworks.

Choosing the right intervention point, every time, comes down to the same question: does this fix the instance, the review step, or the actual generating mechanism — and which of those does this specific case actually need?

title: Lab — Propose and Verify One Systemic Fix
description: Take a finding (from your own prior lab work or a fresh scenario), propose a systemic fix, and produce the before-and-after evidence proving it actually worked.

learningObjectives.text: Propose a systemic fix for a recurring defect and produce verification evidence proving the fix resolved it

contentSections.body: This lab closes the loop this whole module opened: propose a real fix, distinguish pipeline from review-step, and — critically — produce the evidence that it actually worked, not just that it shipped.

contentSections.title: Propose and Verify One Systemic Fix
contentSections.brief: Using a finding from your prior lab work, or the recurring mapping-defect scenario used throughout this module, propose a systemic fix. Decide explicitly whether it's a pipeline fix or a review-step interim measure (and if the latter, what the pipeline fix plan is). Then produce verification evidence — real or realistically constructed — proving the fix resolved the original defect.
contentSections.deliverable: A proposal document: (1) the original defect and its recurrence pattern; (2) the proposed fix, explicitly labeled pipeline or review-step, with reasoning for that choice; (3) if a vendor is involved, a brief escalation summary; (4) before-and-after verification evidence re-running the original known-bad cases against the fixed system.

stages.title: Stage 1 — State the defect and its pattern
stages.instructions: Describe the recurring defect and its occurrence pattern (how many instances, over what period) — reuse feedback-loop evidence from a prior lab if you have it, or construct a realistic pattern of 3+ instances.
stages.checkpoint: You have a defect description with an accumulated pattern, not a single anecdote.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Propose and justify the fix type
stages.instructions: Propose a specific fix. State explicitly whether it's a pipeline fix or a review-step interim measure, and justify the choice using lesson 2's framework — including, if it's an interim measure, what the actual pipeline fix plan and timeline is.
stages.checkpoint: Your proposal names the fix, its type, and the reasoning, with an explicit interim-vs-permanent distinction if relevant.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Handle vendor escalation if relevant
stages.instructions: If the fix requires vendor action, write a brief escalation summary per lesson 4's framework: pattern, safety framing, reproduction steps, relevant contractual/regulatory reference. If no vendor is involved, skip this stage.
stages.checkpoint: Escalation summary written, or explicitly marked not applicable.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Produce verification evidence
stages.instructions: Re-run (or realistically construct the re-run of) the original known-bad cases against the proposed fixed state, and document the before-and-after result for each — confirming the expected output now matches, per lesson 5.
stages.checkpoint: You have explicit before-and-after evidence for each original known-bad case, not just a claim that the fix works.

rubric.criterion: Defect pattern is accumulated, not anecdotal
rubric.meets: The proposal shows a pattern of multiple instances, not a single occurrence treated as the whole case.

rubric.criterion: Fix type is explicit and justified
rubric.meets: Pipeline versus review-step is explicitly stated with reasoning, and if it's interim, the pipeline plan is named.

rubric.criterion: Vendor handling, if applicable, follows the escalation framework
rubric.meets: Pattern, safety framing, and reproduction steps are present in any vendor-facing summary.

rubric.criterion: Verification is evidence, not a claim
rubric.meets: Before-and-after results are shown for each specific known-bad case, not asserted generally.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes instance-level from pipeline-level resolution
rubric.meets: The proposal is explicit about what closes the original instance versus what prevents recurrence.

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole point in one deliverable: a fix isn't done when it's proposed, or even when it's deployed — it's done when you've proven, with the original evidence, that it actually resolved what you found.

title: Checkpoint — Getting the System Fixed
description: Ungraded retrieval — 4 from this module, 4 from the previous module (writing findings), 2 reaching back across the whole phase.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's remediation framework alongside the finding-writing and audit-method standards from earlier in the phase

contentSections.title: What stuck, and what's still there from before
Checkpoint — Getting the System Fixed
contentSections.framing: Ten questions: four from this module, four pulling back to the previous module, and two reaching across the whole phase so far.

questions.prompt: A perfectly written, correctly owned finding sits unresolved for months. What's the most common actual reason, per this module?

options.label: It's competing against other equally valid findings for the same scarce capacity, and nothing forces a prioritization decision
The writing must not have actually been specific enough
It was rated too low in severity by definition

questions.explanation: A well-written finding earns the right to be considered fairly, but writing quality doesn't resolve a capacity or prioritization problem — that requires a different intervention entirely.

questions.prompt: A finding is closed as "resolved" after one chart is manually corrected, but the underlying mapping defect that produced the error is untouched. What's wrong with marking it resolved?

options.label: "Resolved" was applied to the instance-level correction only, leaving the pipeline defect free to keep generating the same error for new patients
Nothing — correcting the chart was the whole point of the finding
The chart should have been corrected by a supervisor instead

questions.explanation: Resolving a finding should answer two separate questions — was the instance corrected, and was the generating defect changed — and closing on the first alone guarantees recurrence.

questions.prompt: What's the key tradeoff between a review-step fix and a pipeline fix for a recurring defect?

options.label: A review-step fix is typically cheaper now but carries an ongoing cost forever; a pipeline fix costs more upfront but eliminates the defect permanently
They're functionally identical in every case
A review-step fix is always superior because it involves human judgment

questions.explanation: A review-step fix manages consequences at an ongoing cost; a pipeline fix removes the generating mechanism at a higher one-time cost — both are legitimate depending on timeline and whether the ambiguity is genuinely resolvable automatically.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a finding be closed on a vendor's or colleague's deployment confirmation alone?

options.label: A deployment confirmation is a claim, not evidence — only re-running the original known-bad cases against the fixed system actually proves the specific defect is resolved
Vendors routinely lie about deployments
It's unnecessary — if something changed, the defect is definitionally gone

questions.explanation: A deployment can be real but narrower than the actual defect, or regress later — verification against the original evidence is what actually closes the loop, not a claim that something shipped.

questions.prompt: What are the four required parts of a complete recommendation, from the writing-findings module?

options.label: A named owner (role), a specific action, a timeframe, and a verification step
A severity rating, an evidence file, a signature, and a due date
A chart ID, a reviewer name, a summary, and a citation

questions.explanation: Owner, action, timeframe, and verification are what turn a recommendation into a trackable task rather than a wish — this module's escalation and fix-verification work builds directly on that structure.

questions.prompt: Why does severity inflation damage a report's credibility over time?

options.label: Once a reader spots even one or two miscalibrated Critical ratings, they start discounting every subsequent rating from that source, accurate or not
It doesn't — more Critical ratings always get more attention
It only matters if a regulator reviews the report

questions.explanation: Inflated severity buys short-term attention at the cost of long-term calibrated trust — a cost that compounds across every future finding from the same source.

questions.prompt: What three anchoring facts does a workable severity scale use instead of adjectives?

options.label: Whether it reached the patient, whether the harm was reversible, and how many steps it was caught from harm
How senior the clinician was, how recent the code is, and how costly the fix would be
The exact code involved, its character length, and its billing weight

questions.explanation: These three facts let independent reviewers land on the same category, and they're the same facts this module's fix-verification work ultimately protects — resolving the defect that produced them.

questions.prompt: In the five-link chain framework from the first module, what's the difference between the origin link and a recovery link?

options.label: The origin is where the wrong fact was created; a recovery link is any later point that could have caught it
They're interchangeable terms for the same thing
The origin is always the patient

questions.explanation: This module's pipeline-versus-instance distinction is the origin/recovery framework applied to remediation: fixing a recovery point (the chart) isn't the same as fixing the origin (the pipeline defect).

questions.prompt: Connecting back to module 1: why is "the coder should have caught the mismapping" an incomplete response to a recurring pipeline defect, using this module's own framework?

options.label: It treats a recovery-link failure as the whole story, the same trap module 1 warned about — it ignores the origin-link defect that will keep generating new instances for the next coder to catch, or miss
It's actually a complete response, since coders are the last line of defense
This only applies to allergy fields, not medication mapping

questions.explanation: Blaming the closest recovery point without fixing the origin is exactly the pattern module 1 introduced and this module has now applied specifically to remediation and closure.

questions.prompt: Connecting back to module 2: why does the evidence-preservation discipline from the audit-method module make this module's fix-verification step cheap rather than expensive?

options.label: Because the original known-bad cases were already captured as durable evidence when the finding was written, verification just means re-running them, not reconstructing them from memory
It doesn't help — verification always requires starting from scratch
Evidence preservation only matters for severity rating, not for verifying fixes later

questions.explanation: The evidence standard from the audit module — durable, reproducible captures rather than paraphrases — is exactly what makes it possible to cheaply re-test the same cases months later, closing the loop this module is built around.

contentSections.body: Getting a system fixed is downstream of everything else in this phase: the chain framework tells you what actually needs fixing, the audit method gives you durable evidence, the writing module gets the finding taken seriously, and this module turns all of that into a change that sticks — and proves it.

title: When a coding tool becomes a regulated device
description: Not every AI-assisted coding feature is regulated the same way — and the line between "documentation aid" and "regulated clinical decision support" is drawn by function, not by what the vendor calls it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a specific AI-assisted coding feature's function places it inside or outside typical clinical decision support regulatory scope

contentSections.title: The line isn't about the label

contentSections.body: A vendor markets their coding tool as "documentation assistance software." A regulator looking at the same tool asks a different question: what does it actually do, and does that function fall inside a regulated category — regardless of what the marketing page calls it.

contentSections.scenario: Compare two features from the same AI-assisted coding product. Feature 1: suggests an ICD-10-CM code from a note, which a human coder reviews and must approve before it's ever stored. Feature 2: automatically adjusts a decision-support alert's sensitivity threshold based on the tool's own confidence in a coded allergy severity, with no human review step before the adjusted threshold takes effect.
contentSections.question: Which feature is more likely to fall under regulatory scrutiny as clinical decision support, and why?

options.label: Feature 1 — because it deals with diagnosis codes, which are inherently more regulated than allergy data
Feature 2 — because it changes what a clinician sees or doesn't see (an alert threshold) with no human review step between the tool's output and a downstream clinical effect
Neither — coding tools are categorically exempt from device regulation

feedback.f1: The presence of a mandatory human review step before anything is stored or acted on is exactly the feature that tends to keep a tool in a lower-scrutiny category — Feature 1's human-in-the-loop design, not the fact that it involves diagnosis codes specifically, is what matters here.
feedback.f2: Right. Feature 2 has no human checkpoint between the tool's own confidence assessment and a real change to what a clinician is alerted about — that's much closer to autonomous clinical decision-making, which is exactly the function regulators focus on regardless of how the overall product is marketed. A coding-suggestion feature with mandatory human review sits in a different risk category from a feature that adjusts alerting behavior on its own.
feedback.neither: Coding and documentation tools are not categorically exempt — some specific functions within a broader product genuinely do fall under device or decision-support regulatory frameworks, and assuming blanket exemption is exactly the mistake this lesson is warning against.

contentSections.concept: **Regulatory scope in this space tends to track function, not product category.** The operative question for any specific feature is: does a human review and approve before it takes clinical effect, or does the tool's output change what happens next on its own? A single product can have some features that clearly require human sign-off (lower scrutiny) sitting next to others that act with more autonomy (higher scrutiny) — and it's a mistake to reason about "the coding tool" as one undifferentiated thing when its individual features may sit in genuinely different regulatory categories.

contentSections.body: This distinction matters concretely for your own audit and governance work: when you're evaluating a pipeline before go-live (this module's later lesson) or classifying a defect's severity, ask feature by feature, not product by product, whether a human reviews and approves before the output has a clinical effect. A tool marketed as a single product might need to be governed as several distinct components with different obligations attached to each — and treating the whole thing as one undifferentiated "coding tool" for governance purposes will either over-scrutinize the low-risk parts or, more dangerously, under-scrutinize the ones that actually change clinical behavior autonomously.

contentSections.question: A vendor updates Feature 1 (the code-suggestion feature with mandatory human review) so that, going forward, codes above a certain confidence score are auto-accepted without review to "save clinician time." Does this change its regulatory posture?
contentSections.answer: Yes, potentially significantly — removing the human review step for high-confidence codes moves that portion of the feature from human-reviewed suggestion toward autonomous action, which is exactly the functional shift this lesson identifies as the trigger for higher scrutiny. This is worth flagging even if the vendor frames it purely as a workflow efficiency improvement.
contentSections.hint: Apply the same functional test from the concept-flow: is there still a human checkpoint before clinical effect?

contentSections.body: Ask feature by feature whether a human reviews and approves before clinical effect, not what the overall product is marketed as. A single tool can span multiple governance categories, and removing a review step — even for 'efficiency' — can shift a feature's category.

contentSections.title: Why this matters for your own work, concretely

contentSections.body: This isn't abstract classification for its own sake — where a feature sits affects what evidence you're obligated to keep, what happens when it changes, and who you have to tell when something goes wrong.

contentSections.scenario: Across real AI-assisted coding products deployed in health systems, a single product commonly bundles multiple distinct features — code suggestion, alert-threshold adjustment, documentation summarization, and others — each with its own actual function.
contentSections.question: In a typical multi-feature AI-assisted coding product, roughly how many of its distinct features, on inspection, actually meet this module's higher-scrutiny (more-autonomous, no-human-checkpoint) test?
contentSections.unit: features (out of a typical 5-8 in a product)
contentSections.explanation: Usually a small minority — often just one or two features (frequently something like an automatic alert-threshold adjustment) act with enough autonomy to meet the higher-scrutiny test, while the majority of features in the same product route through a human review step. This is exactly why governing 'the whole product' as one undifferentiated thing is the wrong unit of analysis: it either drags the low-risk majority into unnecessary rigor, or lets the genuinely higher-risk minority hide inside a product-wide classification that was calibrated to the average feature.

contentSections.body: Three concrete, practical consequences of a feature sitting in a higher-scrutiny category, previewed here and covered in depth over the rest of this module: **validation evidence** the health system should be able to produce showing the feature performs as expected before and during deployment (lesson 2); **change control** — a higher bar for what counts as an update requiring re-validation versus a routine patch (lesson 3); and **incident reporting** — an obligation to report certain categories of safety-relevant failure, potentially to the vendor and a regulator, not just to your internal safety committee (lesson 4). None of these obligations apply uniformly to "the coding tool" as a whole — they attach to specific functions based on what those functions actually do.

Where a specific feature sits governs what validation evidence, change-control rigor, and incident-reporting obligations actually apply to it — these aren't abstract classifications, they're the concrete requirements the rest of this module walks through.

title: Validation evidence a health system should have and often doesn't
description: "The vendor says it's validated" is not validation evidence a health system holds itself — and the gap between those two things is where a lot of real risk quietly lives.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a health system's validation evidence for an AI-assisted coding feature is adequate or merely a restated vendor claim

contentSections.body: A vendor's marketing materials cite a validation study: 96% accuracy on a benchmark dataset. Ask what accuracy the tool achieves on your health system's actual patient population, actual documentation style, actual specialty mix — and the honest answer, most of the time, is that nobody has checked.

contentSections.scenario: A health system deploys an AI-assisted coding tool relying entirely on the vendor's published validation study, performed on a different health system's data with a different patient population and documentation style. Six months post-deployment, an internal audit (using this phase's methods) finds a meaningfully higher error rate than the vendor's published figure.
contentSections.question: What's the actual gap that let this happen?

options.label: The vendor's original study was fraudulent

A validation study performed on one population doesn't automatically transfer to a different population with different documentation patterns, specialty mix, and patient demographics — and nobody validated it against this specific deployment
The internal audit methodology must have been flawed, since the vendor's study should be more authoritative

feedback.fraud: Fraud is rare and not the typical explanation — a legitimate, honestly-conducted validation study on one population can still simply not generalize well to a different one, which is the far more common and important mechanism to understand.
feedback.generalization: Right. Documentation conventions, specialty mix, patient demographics, and even which EHR templates are in use all affect how well an AI-assisted coding tool performs — a study on a different population is real evidence about that population, not a guarantee about yours. This is exactly why your own audit work, using this phase's methods, matters even for a 'validated' tool.
feedback.audit_flawed: This gets the authority question backwards — a rigorous internal audit using stratified sampling and anchored severity, as this phase has taught, is directly measuring your own population's actual performance, which is more relevant to your patients than a study on a different population, not less.

contentSections.mechanism: **A vendor's validation study is evidence about the vendor's test population, not a guarantee about yours.** The gap between "the vendor validated it" and "we've validated it for our population" is exactly where undetected risk accumulates — and it's a gap your own audit work, from earlier in this phase, is what actually closes.

contentSections.body: A workable minimum validation evidence set a health system should hold itself, not just cite from a vendor: **a local performance baseline** — an initial audit, using this phase's sampling and severity methods, run against your own population before or shortly after go-live; **ongoing performance tracking** — periodic re-sampling (echoing the regression-check discipline from the last module) rather than a single point-in-time check; and **a documented comparison** between the vendor's claimed performance and your own measured performance, with any meaningful gap explained or escalated. None of this requires re-inventing anything — it's this phase's audit method, applied specifically to produce the evidence a governance review will ask for.

A vendor's validation study is evidence about their test population. A health system needs its own local performance baseline and ongoing tracking — produced by exactly the audit methods this phase has already taught.
This gap is common enough to be worth naming plainly, not as a hypothetical failure mode but as a routine finding.

contentSections.scenario: Reviewing a health system's governance file for an AI-assisted coding tool that's been live for two years.
contentSections.question: Which of these, if found in the file, would actually satisfy the local-validation-evidence standard from this lesson?

items.label: A copy of the vendor's published validation study, filed as "validation evidence"
A dated internal audit report, using stratified sampling, measuring error rate on this health system's own charts
A sales presentation slide citing the same 96% accuracy figure
A record of quarterly re-sampling showing performance trend over the two years live
A meeting note recording that the vendor 'assured us the tool is safe'

explanation.vendor_study: No — filing the vendor's study as your own validation evidence is exactly the gap this lesson is naming. It's relevant context, not a substitute for your own measurement.
explanation.local_audit: Yes — this is the actual local performance baseline the standard calls for, produced using this phase's own audit methods against your real population.
explanation.sales_deck: No — a sales artifact restating a vendor claim isn't independent evidence regardless of how many times it's cited across different documents.
explanation.periodic_resample: Yes — ongoing tracking over time is what catches drift and regression (echoing the previous module's fix-verification discipline), rather than treating a single go-live check as permanently sufficient.
explanation.verbal_assurance: No — an unverified assurance, even recorded in good faith, carries none of the evidentiary weight this phase has spent two modules establishing that a real finding needs.

contentSections.synthesis: A governance file with only vendor-sourced documents in it, however many of them there are, doesn't actually contain local validation evidence — the test is simple: was this specific health system's own population ever independently measured, and is that measurement kept current.

contentSections.body: A governance file full of vendor-sourced documents, however extensive, isn't local validation evidence. The test: was this health system's own population independently measured, and is that measurement kept current.

title: Model updates in a regulated setting
description: A vendor's routine model update can be a genuinely different product overnight — and treating every update the same, whether it's a bug fix or a retrained model, is how a validated system quietly stops being validated.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an update requiring re-validation from one that doesn't, using a functional risk framework rather than the vendor's own labeling

contentSections.body: "Version 4.2 — minor update, performance improvements" reads like nothing to worry about. It's also exactly the kind of release note that has, in real systems, quietly retrained the underlying model on new data with materially different behavior — and "minor" described the version number bump, not the actual scope of what changed.

contentSections.code:
Change-control policy (as written):

  Any update labeled 'major' by the vendor triggers
  full re-validation before deployment.
  Updates labeled 'minor' or 'patch' are deployed
  automatically without additional review.
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this policy?

options.label: It doesn't specify a deployment timeline
It outsources the risk classification entirely to the vendor's own versioning convention, which reflects the vendor's release process, not the actual functional risk of what changed
Full re-validation should never be required for any update

feedback.timeline: A timeline gap is a real but secondary issue — the deeper flaw is that the policy's entire risk classification hinges on a label the vendor assigns for their own reasons, which may have nothing to do with your actual re-validation needs.
feedback.outsourced: Right. A vendor's "major/minor/patch" labeling reflects their own release and semantic-versioning conventions — it says nothing reliable about whether the update changed the model's underlying behavior in a way that matters for your patients. A model retrain, a change to a confidence threshold, or a shift in what counts as a match can all ship under a "minor" label if the vendor's versioning scheme doesn't track functional risk the way your governance policy needs it to.
feedback.never: Full re-validation is genuinely unnecessary for many updates — a UI text change or a genuine bug fix with no behavioral effect on coding output doesn't need it. The flaw isn't that re-validation is ever required, it's that the trigger for requiring it is outsourced to the wrong signal.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A workable change-control policy classifies updates by **functional risk to your patients**, not by the vendor's version label: does this update change what codes get suggested, what confidence thresholds trigger review, what data the model was trained or retrained on, or what alerts fire? Any "yes" to those questions warrants at least a targeted re-check — re-running a sample of your own known cases (the same discipline as fix verification from the last module) — regardless of whether the vendor called it major, minor, or a patch.

contentSections.body: In practice this means asking the vendor a specific question on every release, not accepting their label at face value: **did this update change the model's outputs, training data, or decision thresholds in any way that could affect coding results?** A vendor with a mature process will be able to answer this directly. A vendor who can only point you back to their own major/minor labeling is itself a signal worth noting — it suggests their release process may not track the distinction your governance actually needs.

contentSections.question: A vendor ships a 'patch' release that, per their own release notes, 'improves allergy classification accuracy.' Does the word 'improves' mean this update is safe to skip re-checking?
contentSections.answer: No — 'improves' still means the model's behavior changed, which is exactly the functional-risk trigger from this lesson, regardless of whether the change is an improvement on average. An improvement on average can still shift behavior on specific edge cases your population has more of than the vendor's general test set — which is precisely what a targeted re-check against your own known cases would catch.
contentSections.hint: The trigger for re-checking is whether behavior changed, not whether the change is framed as positive or negative.

contentSections.body: Classify update risk by whether it changes model outputs, training data, or decision thresholds — never by the vendor's own major/minor/patch label, which reflects their release process, not your patients' risk.

contentSections.title: Building a lightweight re-check into the update process

contentSections.body: Full re-validation on every update isn't realistic — vendors ship updates frequently, and treating every one as a from-scratch validation event would grind the relationship, and your own capacity, to a halt. The answer is a tiered response, not an all-or-nothing one.

contentSections.intro: Design a tiered update-response process that avoids both extremes — treating every update as trivial, and treating every update as requiring full re-validation.

fields.prompt: What's the right response to an update the vendor confirms changed nothing about model outputs, thresholds, or training data (e.g. a UI fix)?
options: Deploy without additional review — no functional risk trigger was hit
Full re-validation regardless
Ignore the update entirely and don't deploy it
fields.correctValue: Deploy without additional review — no functional risk trigger was hit
fields.feedback: When the vendor confirms, specifically, that nothing behavioral changed, there's no functional-risk trigger and no reason to add review overhead.

fields.prompt: What's the right response to an update that did change model outputs or thresholds, but in a way the vendor characterizes as a narrow, specific fix?
options: A targeted re-check: re-run your own known-case sample (per the fix-verification discipline) against the new version before or shortly after deployment
Full re-validation from scratch, treating it identically to a major model overhaul
No action needed since it's 'just a fix'
fields.correctValue: A targeted re-check: re-run your own known-case sample (per the fix-verification discipline) against the new version before or shortly after deployment
fields.feedback: A targeted re-check calibrated to the actual scope of what changed is the proportionate response — enough to catch a problem without treating every behavioral update as a full re-validation event.

fields.prompt: What's the right response to a full model retrain on new data?
options: Full re-validation, treating it functionally as a new deployment, including a fresh local performance baseline
The same targeted re-check as a narrow fix
Automatic deployment, since retrains are usually improvements
fields.correctValue: Full re-validation, treating it functionally as a new deployment, including a fresh local performance baseline
fields.feedback: A retrain can shift behavior broadly and unpredictably across the whole system, which is functionally a new product from a validation standpoint — this is the case the 'major update' tier exists for, regardless of what the vendor calls it.

contentSections.synthesis: Three tiers, sized to actual risk: no functional change needs no extra review; a narrow behavioral change needs a targeted re-check against your own known cases; a retrain or broad behavioral shift needs full re-validation. The vendor's own major/minor label should inform, but never substitute for, this classification.

contentSections.body: A tiered response — no review, targeted re-check, or full re-validation, sized to actual functional risk — keeps governance realistic without letting genuinely significant updates slip through under a misleading vendor label.

title: Incident reporting obligations
description: A patient-safety-relevant AI coding failure isn't just an internal finding to fix quietly — depending on its nature, it may carry a reporting obligation that exists independently of whether you've already resolved it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a specific incident meets the threshold for external reporting versus internal-only resolution

contentSections.title: Fixed internally is not the same as no reporting obligation

contentSections.body: A team finds and fixes a serious coding defect within a week, before it reaches a regulator's radar through any other channel, and treats the fast internal resolution as the end of the matter. Speed of internal fix and the existence of an external reporting obligation are two separate questions, and answering the first one well doesn't answer the second.

contentSections.scenario: Using this phase's anchored severity scale, a coding defect is rated Critical — it reached a patient and caused harm that was not reversible. The internal team fixed the pipeline defect within a week and verified the fix per the previous module's discipline.
contentSections.question: Does the fast, well-verified internal resolution change whether this incident needs to be reported externally (to a vendor, and potentially a regulator, depending on how the feature is classified)?

options.label: Yes — a resolved incident no longer needs to be reported, since the problem is already fixed
No — the reporting obligation, where one exists, is generally triggered by what happened (a Critical-severity event involving a regulated function), not by whether it was later fixed quickly
It depends only on whether the patient or family files a complaint

feedback.no_longer: This is a natural but incorrect assumption — a fast, well-handled internal fix is exactly the kind of response a reporting system exists to learn about, not a reason to avoid telling anyone. Reporting obligations generally attach to what happened, not to how quickly it was subsequently resolved.
feedback.still_applies: Right. If a specific incident's severity and the function involved meet a reporting threshold, fixing it quickly and well doesn't retroactively remove that threshold — it's a separate track. This module's earlier lesson on regulated functions is exactly why this matters: a Critical event involving a function that falls under decision-support-adjacent scrutiny may carry an obligation regardless of how fast your own team responded.
feedback.complaint: Reporting obligations for safety-relevant defects in this space typically aren't contingent on a patient or family complaint — they can exist independently of whether anyone outside the health system ever becomes aware something went wrong, which is exactly why relying on 'nobody complained' as a filter is a governance risk in itself.

contentSections.concept: **A reporting obligation, where one applies, is triggered by what happened and what function was involved — not by how well or how fast you fixed it afterward.** This is a genuinely uncomfortable fact for teams that take pride in fast internal response, and it's exactly why it needs to be said plainly rather than left as an assumption: good internal remediation and an external reporting obligation are not substitutes for each other.

contentSections.body: The practical takeaway isn't to memorize a specific regulatory citation — reporting frameworks and thresholds vary by jurisdiction, by how a given feature is classified (per lesson 1's functional test), and by evolving guidance, and a health system's compliance or legal team, not an individual reviewer, should make the final reporting determination. The reviewer's job is narrower and still critical: **flag any Critical-severity finding (per this phase's anchored scale) involving a function that plausibly falls under regulated decision-support scope for a compliance review, as a matter of course, before internal resolution is treated as closing the matter.** Making that flag automatic, rather than a judgment call made under the pressure of an already-resolved incident, is what keeps this from quietly getting skipped.

Flag Critical-severity findings involving plausibly-regulated functions for compliance review as standard process, regardless of how quickly they were fixed internally. The reporting question is separate from the fix-quality question, and needs its own answer.

contentSections.title: Not crying wolf on reporting, either

contentSections.body: The lesson so far could be read as "report everything, to be safe." That's not quite right either, and it echoes the severity-inflation problem from earlier in this phase in a new context.

contentSections.question: A Medium-severity finding (a near-miss caught two steps before harm) involves a function that clearly falls under regulated decision-support scope. Should it be automatically flagged for compliance review using the criteria from this lesson?
contentSections.answer: Not automatically under this specific flag — the criteria require both Critical severity and regulated function together, and this is Medium severity. That doesn't mean it's unimportant (it may well warrant the urgency-note treatment from the writing-findings module), but conflating every regulated-function finding with a reporting-obligation flag, regardless of severity, is exactly the over-flagging this lesson is warning against.
contentSections.hint: Check both criteria from the lesson's flag rule, not just one of them.

contentSections.body: Just as inflating severity ratings erodes a report's credibility, treating every finding as reportable regardless of its actual severity and function erodes the compliance-review process's ability to prioritize the things that genuinely need it — and it puts real strain on a process meant for a specific category of event. The discipline is the same one this whole phase has been building: **use the anchored facts.** Was it Critical severity, by the reached-patient/reversibility/steps-from-harm standard from the audit-method module? Does it involve a function that plausibly meets the regulated-decision-support test from lesson 1? Both, together, are the flag criteria — not "this felt serious" and not "this technically touched a coded field."

Flag for compliance review on both criteria together — Critical severity and plausibly regulated function — not either alone. Over-flagging degrades the process's ability to prioritize the same way severity inflation degrades a report.

title: Questions to ask before a pipeline goes live
description: Every question in this phase, asked in advance instead of discovered in an audit six months later, is cheaper by an order of magnitude — this lesson turns the phase's whole toolkit into a pre-go-live checklist.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a pre-go-live governance checklist that applies this phase's frameworks proactively rather than reactively

contentSections.title: Everything this phase taught, asked before deployment instead of after

contentSections.body: Every framework in this phase — the chain, the audit method, the finding standard, the remediation approach, and now regulatory classification — has been reactive: something already happened, now diagnose and fix it. This lesson asks the same questions before go-live, when the cost of getting an answer is a checklist item instead of a patient.

contentSections.question: A new AI-assisted coding pipeline is proposed for deployment. Order these pre-go-live questions from earliest-answerable (should be resolved before any other question makes sense) to latest.
steps: Which specific features involve a human review step before clinical effect, and which act more autonomously? (module 5, lesson 1's functional classification)
For the higher-scrutiny features, what local validation evidence do we have, or need to generate, against our own population? (lesson 2)
What's our tiered response plan for future vendor updates to this pipeline? (lesson 3)
What's our process for flagging and routing a Critical-severity, regulated-function incident to compliance review if one occurs? (lesson 4)
contentSections.explanation: Functional classification has to come first, because every later question depends on knowing which features are higher-scrutiny — you can't scope validation evidence, an update-response tier, or an incident-reporting process without first knowing which features they apply to. Validation evidence comes next because it's the immediate go-live gate. The update-response plan and incident-reporting process are both about the system's ongoing life after go-live, which is why they come last — but notably, both need to be *decided* before go-live, not improvised after the first update ships or the first incident occurs.

contentSections.body: Classify function first — it's the input every other pre-go-live question depends on. Validation evidence gates go-live itself; update-response and incident-reporting plans need to exist before go-live even though they govern what happens after.

contentSections.title: The checklist a health system could actually use

contentSections.body: This is the module's lab, previewed: the deliverable is a real, usable checklist, not a restatement of the phase in prose.

contentSections.question: A go-live proposal answers all five checklist categories except one, which is marked "TBD — will figure out later." Should the review committee approve go-live conditional on filling that in afterward?
contentSections.answer: No — per this lesson's standard, a "no" or "unclear" answer to any of the five items is a real go-live blocker, not a note for later. Approving conditionally on a "TBD" treats the checklist as a formality rather than the gate it's meant to be, and it's exactly the kind of deferral that turns into never happening once the pipeline is already live and other priorities take over.
contentSections.hint: Recall the lesson's explicit statement about what a missing checklist answer means for go-live readiness.

contentSections.body: A pre-go-live checklist worth actually using is short enough to get read and specific enough to force a real answer, not a checkbox. For each proposed pipeline or feature, at minimum: **(1) Function** — does this act with human review before clinical effect, or more autonomously? **(2) Local validation** — do we have our own population's performance data, not just the vendor's, and is there a plan for ongoing re-sampling? **(3) Update tiering** — is there an agreed process for classifying future vendor updates by functional risk rather than their labeling? **(4) Incident routing** — is there a standing process for flagging Critical-severity, regulated-function incidents to compliance, independent of how fast they get fixed internally? **(5) Chain mapping** — using module 1's framework, has someone actually traced what this pipeline could get wrong and which downstream systems would inherit that error? A "no" or "unclear" answer to any of these is a real go-live blocker, not a note for later — every one of them is dramatically cheaper to answer now than to reconstruct after an incident.

A usable pre-go-live checklist has five real questions — function, local validation, update tiering, incident routing, chain mapping — each demanding an actual answer, not a checkbox. This is the entire phase, turned proactive.

Checkpoint — Governance and Regulation
contentSections.framing: Ten questions: four from this module, four pulling back to the previous module, and two reaching across the whole phase.

questions.prompt: What determines whether a specific AI-assisted coding feature falls under higher regulatory scrutiny?

options.label: Its function — specifically, whether a human reviews and approves before it takes clinical effect, or it acts more autonomously
What the vendor's marketing materials call the overall product
Whether it involves diagnosis codes specifically, as opposed to other coded fields

questions.explanation: Scrutiny tracks function, not product labeling or field type — a single product can span multiple categories depending on whether individual features have a human checkpoint before clinical effect.

questions.prompt: Why isn't a vendor's published validation study sufficient as a health system's own validation evidence?

options.label: It's evidence about the vendor's test population, which may not generalize to a different population's documentation patterns, specialty mix, and demographics
Vendor studies are generally fraudulent
It is sufficient — no additional local evidence is needed if the vendor's study is legitimate

questions.explanation: Legitimate validation on one population doesn't guarantee equivalent performance on a different one — a health system needs its own local baseline, produced using this phase's own audit methods.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a vendor's major/minor/patch version labeling be used as the trigger for re-validation decisions?

options.label: It reflects the vendor's release conventions, not the functional risk of what actually changed in the model's behavior
Vendors never label updates accurately on purpose
Every update should get full re-validation regardless of label

questions.explanation: A 'minor' label can still ship a behavioral change, like a retrain or threshold shift, that matters clinically — risk should be classified by whether outputs, training data, or thresholds changed, not by the vendor's own versioning scheme.

questions.prompt: What's the dual criteria for flagging an incident for compliance review, per this module?

options.label: Critical severity (by the anchored facts) together with a plausibly regulated function — not either alone
Any finding that technically touched a coded field, regardless of severity
Only incidents a patient or family has already complained about

questions.explanation: Flagging on both criteria together avoids both under-reporting (missing a genuine Critical, regulated-function event) and over-flagging (which degrades the process the same way severity inflation degrades a report).

questions.prompt: What's the key tradeoff between a review-step fix and a pipeline fix for a recurring defect, from the previous module?

options.label: A review-step fix is cheaper now but carries an ongoing cost forever; a pipeline fix costs more upfront but eliminates the defect permanently
They are functionally identical in every case
A review-step fix always permanently eliminates the defect

questions.explanation: This is the same distinction this module's update-tiering lesson echoes: a targeted re-check versus full re-validation trades cost and thoroughness in a structurally similar way.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a finding be closed on a vendor's deployment confirmation alone?

options.label: A deployment confirmation is a claim, not evidence — only re-running the original known-bad cases against the fixed system actually proves the specific defect is resolved
Vendors routinely misrepresent deployments
It's unnecessary once something has changed

questions.explanation: The same evidence discipline from earlier in the phase applies to closing a finding as to opening one — a claim needs verification, not just trust.

questions.prompt: What are the four required parts of a complete recommendation, from the writing-findings module?

options.label: A named owner (role), a specific action, a timeframe, and a verification step
A severity rating, an evidence file, a signature, and a due date
A chart ID, a reviewer name, a summary, and a citation

questions.explanation: Owner, action, timeframe, and verification turn a recommendation into a trackable task — the same structure this module's pre-go-live checklist items are built to satisfy.

questions.prompt: Connecting back to module 1: how does this module's chain-mapping checklist item use the original five-link framework?

options.label: It applies the same origin-to-patient chain analysis proactively, before deployment, instead of reactively after an incident has already occurred
It replaces the chain framework with a new, unrelated regulatory model
Chain mapping only applies to allergy and medication fields, not to governance

questions.explanation: The pre-go-live checklist's chain-mapping item is the same code/record/decision-support/clinician/patient framework from module 1, run in advance to find likely failure points before they produce real harm.

questions.prompt: Connecting back to module 2: why does this module's local-validation-evidence standard rely on the same stratified sampling method from the audit-method module rather than a simple random sample?

options.label: Because validation needs to characterize performance on the highest-risk populations and fields specifically, not just an average across the whole system — the same reason a safety audit stratifies rather than samples randomly
